_note: Two modes. STRICT = required_prerequisite + transformation: the only edges that may support roots, depth or reach. GROWTH = preferred_substrate / replacement_opportunity / co_presence: preference and opportunity, counted as observed relationships, never as dependencies. Every edge carries evidence.basis, evidence.cites and evidence.certainty.

nodes.description: Ag₂S — monoclinic silver sulfide and the most important silver ore on Earth at 87% Ag by weight. Lead-gray to iron-black metallic, Mohs 2-2.5, sectile (cuts like lead). The cold-storage form: above 173°C the same composition crystallizes as cubic argentite, and most acanthite in nature is paramorphic after cooled argentite, retaining the cubic external form while the lattice underneath inverts to monoclinic (Petruk et al. 1974, Canadian Mineralogist 12). Forms in low-sulfidation epithermal veins, mesothermal silver veins, and supergene enrichment zones; classic localities include Guanajuato (Mexico, pseudo-cubic crystals), Freiberg (Saxony), and Kongsberg (Norway).

Ca₂(Mg,Fe)₅Si₈O₂₂(OH)₂ — monoclinic Ca-Mg-Fe amphibole; Fe-bearing intermediate of the tremolite-actinolite series. H 5-6, density 3.0-3.4, green to dark-green characteristic color from Fe²⁺ M-site crystal field. Forms in greenschist-facies metamorphism + hydrothermal alteration + retrograde skarn. NEPHRITE-JADE variety (the more important of the two gem 'jade' minerals; jadeite is the other) is the compact felted-fibrous form — Maori pounamu (New Zealand), Chinese imperial jade (Hetian White Jade is the most famous actinolite nephrite), Cassiar BC + Wyoming USA + Italian Alps. Also the ACTINOLITE-ASBESTOS commercial variety (one of six WHO-recognized asbestos minerals). Trace Cr produces 'smaragdite' chromian-green actinolite (gem grade). Discriminator from tremolite: Fe ≥ ~30 ppm. Refs: Hawthorne FC et al. (2012) Am. Min. 97:2031; Wilson DGD & Yi-Lin S (2018) on nephrite jade chemistry; Anthony Handbook v.IIB.

Zn₂(AsO₄)(OH), a supergene arsenate from oxidizing Zn-As sulfide ores. Classic Ojuela Mine (Mexico) habit: yellow-green prismatic sprays. Cu-substituted zones (cuproadamite) fluoresce brilliant apple-green under SW UV — but heavy Cu quenches the glow, creating striking fluorescent/non-fluorescent crystal pairs.

NaAlSi₃O₈, the sodium end-member of the plagioclase series. Platy cleavelandite is the pegmatite signature habit. Fine albite/oligoclase exsolution lamellae scatter light into blue-white adularescence — the moonstone shimmer.

KAl₃(SO₄)₂(OH)₆, the K-Al sister of jarosite (alunite group, isostructural). The index mineral of 'advanced argillic' alteration in porphyry-Cu lithocaps and high-sulfidation epithermal Au deposits — when geologists say a porphyry has a 'lithocap', alunite + kaolinite + pyrophyllite + dickite are the diagnostic phases of the kilometers-wide acid-altered horizon above the intrusion. Type locality Marysvale (Utah), where alunite was mined as a K-fertilizer source 1915-1930s before Carlsbad potash made K cheaper to mine elsewhere. World-class epithermal-Au localities: Goldfield (Nevada), Summitville (Colorado), Tambo (Chile), Yanacocha (Peru), Nansatsu district (Japan). ⁴⁰Ar/³⁹Ar geochronology preserves the K-Ar age of the acid-sulfate hydrothermal event, critical for porphyry-system timing (Stoffregen et al. 2000).

~(Fe,Mg)₇Si₈O₂₂(OH)₂ — Fe-DOMINANT cummingtonite-grunerite asbestiform variety. "BROWN ASBESTOS" of commerce. Type-locality Penge, Transvaal South Africa (also Cape Province + Witbank); minor production in India (Roro) and US (Montana). Monoclinic C2/m. H 5-6, density 3.1-3.6, brown-to-yellow-brown silky fiber bundles. One of six WHO-recognized commercial asbestos minerals; less carcinogenic than crocidolite but still classified as Group 1 carcinogen (IARC). The 'amosite' name is specifically the asbestiform commercial variety ("Asbestos Mines of South Africa"); non-asbestiform cummingtonite is a separate mineralogical name. Distinct from anthophyllite by structure (monoclinic vs orthorhombic) + by Fe-dominance. Refs: Hawthorne FC et al. (2012) Am. Min. 97:2031; Anthony Handbook v.IIB; Hodgson AA (1965) Mineralogy of South African amphibole asbestos. CSIR Report; Frank DR et al. (2002).

Al₂SiO₅ — orthorhombic (Pnnm), the LOW-PRESSURE aluminosilicate polymorph (kyanite is the high-pressure form, sillimanite the high-temperature; the three meet at the Al₂SiO₅ triple point, ~500°C / 0.4 GPa, Holdaway 1971 Am.J.Sci 271:97). Coarse near-SQUARE {110} prisms — the two {110} cleavages intersect at ~89°. The index mineral of low-pressure contact-metamorphic aluminous metapelites — hornfels in the aureole of a shallow intrusion — and of low-P regional (Buchan / Abukuma) terranes. Pink-rose to pinkish-brown from Mn³⁺ (the green viridine variety is Mn-rich); chrome-green where Cr substitutes. CHIASTOLITE is the variety grown in a GRAPHITIC (carbon-bearing) metapelite: carbonaceous matter is swept into the rapidly-growing CORNER growth sectors of the square prism, so a cross-section shows a dark Maltese cross — growth-SECTOR zoning, not concentric banding (Dowty 1976 Am.Min. 61:460; Mason et al. 2010 Gondwana Research 18(1):222-229, quartz+graphite co-precipitation in a graphite-buffered H₂O–CO₂ fluid). Also a member of the hottest advanced-argillic alteration (quartz-andalusite, ~360-400°C) in porphyry lithocaps (Sillitoe 2010).

PbSO₄ — orthorhombic, brilliant adamantine luster (one of the most lustrous non-metallic minerals). Intermediate step in the lead oxidation sequence: galena → anglesite → cerussite. Forms at the first wave of oxidation when sulfide-S becomes sulfate-S; transient in carbonate groundwater, where it dissolves and reprecipitates as cerussite. Named for Anglesey island (Wales) where the type specimens were found.

CaSO₄, the anhydrous calcium sulfate; sister of selenite/gypsum (CaSO₄·2H₂O). The anhydrite-gypsum boundary is not a single line but an XY plot of T vs salinity (Hardie 1967): in pure water anhydrite stable above 60°C, but in saline brines (>100‰ NaCl-eq) anhydrite stable down to surface T due to lowered water activity. Two distinct geological occurrences: (1) high-T hydrothermal (porphyry-Cu deep-brine zones at 200-700°C — Bingham Roedder 1971); (2) low-T evaporite (Persian Gulf / Coorong sabkha + Salar de Atacama — anhydrite + halite + dolomite stratigraphy). Below 60°C in dilute fluid, anhydrite is metastable and rehydrates to gypsum/selenite. Naica's Cave of Crystals shows exactly this: an older anhydrite floor preserved from the deeper brine phase, overgrown by giant selenite blades when the cave dewatered + cooled. Industrial: cement-setting accelerator, sulfur source, plaster manufacture (anhydrite ↔ gypsum hydration cycle). Pale-lavender 'angelite' Peruvian variety is a metaphysical-stone fixture.

Ni₃(AsO₄)₂·8H₂O — 'nickel bloom,' the apple-green Ni equivalent of erythrite. Same vivianite-group structure, same supergene origin; nickel substitutes for cobalt and the color shifts from crimson to apple-green. Mg substitution produces the pale cabrerite variety; Co substitution pinks it toward erythrite. Dehydrates above 200°C.

(Mg,Fe)₇Si₈O₂₂(OH)₂ — ORTHORHOMBIC (Pnma) Mg-Fe orthoamphibole. NO Ca — discriminator vs the calcic amphiboles tremolite/actinolite. H 5.5-6, density 2.85-3.6, brown to grey-brown color. Forms in: ultramafic-host serpentinite-pegmatite-gneiss settings (Finland type — Kongsberg + Falun; Carolina + Georgia USA; Cyprus ophiolite); cordierite-anthophyllite gneisses (medium-grade metamorphic). COMMONLY ASBESTIFORM — anthophyllite-asbestos is one of six WHO-recognized commercial asbestos minerals (Cherokee NC + Bolt's Quarry Vermont were US commercial sources). Less commercially significant than chrysotile or crocidolite but historically used. The Carolina + Georgia anthophyllite-talc deposits are the historical US source. Discriminator from amosite: orthorhombic vs monoclinic; lower Fe-dominance. Refs: Hawthorne FC et al. (2012) Am. Min. 97:2031; Anthony Handbook v.IIB; Robinson P et al. (1971) — amphibole-talc rocks.

Cu₃(SO₄)(OH)₄, the dry-acid end of the brochantite ↔ antlerite Cu-sulfate fork (pH 1-3.5 stability). Same emerald-green color as brochantite — visually indistinguishable in hand specimen — distinguished by chemistry (Cu₃ vs Cu₄, more SO₄ per Cu unit) and acid-resistance test (antlerite dissolves in dilute HCl; brochantite resists). Type locality Antler mine (Mohave County, Arizona — Hillebrand 1889). World-class deposits at Chuquicamata (Chile) where antlerite was the dominant supergene Cu mineral mined 1920s-50s before the deeper hypogene chalcocite zone became the modern target. Coexists with brochantite + atacamite + chalcanthite at most Atacama supergene Cu deposits. The pH-fork mechanism (Pollard et al. 1992) is the most diagnostic chemistry in arid-supergene Cu mineralogy.

Ca5(PO4)3(F,Cl,OH) — the structural archetype of the apatite supergroup (parent of pyromorphite, mimetite, vanadinite). Mohs hardness reference at 5. Forms in nearly every geological environment — magmatic accessory, pegmatite late-stage, hydrothermal vein, metamorphic skarn, sedimentary phosphorite, biological. Color span is the widest of any common mineral: green, blue, violet, yellow, brown depending on Mn²⁺, REE, Fe²⁺ activators. Fluorescent under UV in most varieties via Mn²⁺ + Eu²⁺ + Sm³⁺ + Ce³⁺ activator soup.

KCa₄Si₈O₂₀(F,OH)·8H₂O — a tetragonal sheet silicate (technically phyllosilicate) classed with the zeolites for its hydrated, low-T vesicle-filling behavior. Stage III Deccan Traps mineral per Ottens et al. 2019: forms 21–58 Ma post-eruption when alkaline groundwater finally percolates through cooled basalt vesicles. Pseudo-cubic tabular blocks with perfect {001} cleavage. Hematite-needle phantom inclusions produce the prized 'bloody apophyllite' variety from Nashik. The Pune/Pashan GREEN variety owes its colour to V⁴⁺ (~1600 ppm in the lattice; Rossman 1974, Am.Min. 59:621-622), dichroic and, to the eye, a uniform green body colour — a provenance-locked image corpus of Pune specimens (2026-06-21) shows no visible prism-vs-pyramid sector partition. Apophyllite IS genuinely sector-zoned, but only optically (anomalous birefringence, crossed-polars); the visible green is even, so it is rendered uniform with a pearly {001} basal-face luster, not a colour hourglass. The name (Greek apo + phylliso, 'to flake apart') records the perfect {001} basal cleavage and the way crystals exfoliate and whiten on heating as they lose zeolitic water.

Be₃Al₂Si₆O₁₈ with Fe²⁺ — the blue variety of beryl. Most abundant gem beryl variety; every gem-producing pegmatite yields aquamarine. Santa Maria (Pakistan Shigar) is the deep-blue benchmark; Cruzeiro and Padre Paraíso (Brazil Minas Gerais) are the volume producers. Fires when Fe ≥ 8 ppm in the Fe²⁺ state (non-oxidizing).

CaCO₃ in the orthorhombic crystal system — the metastable polymorph of calcite. Same composition, different structure, kinetically favored over thermodynamically-stable calcite when (Folk 1974, Morse 1997, Sun 2015): Mg/Ca > ~1.5 (dominant control — Mg poisons calcite growth steps but is excluded from aragonite's orthorhombic structure); T > ~50°C in low-Mg waters; supersaturation Ω > ~10 (Ostwald step rule); or trace Sr/Pb/Ba present (these cations match Ca²⁺ in aragonite's 9-fold coordination but not calcite's 6-fold). At surface pressure aragonite is metastable — over geologic time it converts to calcite (half-life ~10⁵ yr at 25°C, ~10³ yr at 80°C, faster in hot wet systems).

Ag₂S — body-centered cubic silver sulfide, the high-temperature polymorph stable only above 173°C. A ghost mineral: every argentite specimen at room temperature is actually acanthite (monoclinic) wearing argentite's cubic crystal habit, because below 173°C the lattice inverts in place while the external form stays frozen — handled by the apply_paramorph_transitions hook in vugg.py. Lead-gray to black metallic, Mohs 2-2.5, sectile. Forms in the high-T zones of epithermal and mesothermal Ag-bearing veins; classic localities include Comstock Lode (Nevada), Pachuca-Real del Monte (Mexico), and Freiberg (Saxony). Source: research/minerals/research-argentite.md (boss commit f2939da), Petruk et al. 1974.

FeAsS, the arsenic gateway mineral and the #1 gold-trapping mineral. Mesothermal primary sulfide (300-500°C, reducing); silver-white metallic prisms with diamond cross-section, deep longitudinal striations. Emits garlic odor when struck (As vapor — diagnostic). Structurally traps Au up to ~1500 ppm as 'invisible gold' (Reich et al. 2005; Cook & Chryssoulis 1990) — released to fluid on supergene oxidation, producing the orogenic Au-enrichment signature (Graeme et al. 2019 for Bisbee). Oxidation pathway: FeAsS + O₂ + H₂O → Fe³⁺ + AsO₄³⁻ + H₂SO₄ → feeds scorodite + acidifies.

Cu2Cl(OH)3 — the chloride end-member of the supergene Cu oxidation suite. Forms in arid Cu-porphyry zones where seawater or saline groundwater delivers Cl⁻ and the dry climate prevents the carbonate (malachite/azurite) and sulfate (brochantite/antlerite) phases from winning. Color is the most intense emerald-green of any common mineral — Cu²⁺ chromophore in distorted octahedral coordination. Atacama Desert is the type locality and the climate ideal: rain-shadow aridity + Cu sulfide oxidation + chloride-rich groundwater. Also forms on bronze artifacts in seawater (Antikythera mechanism, sunken Greek statues).

(Zn,Cu)₅(CO₃)₂(OH)₆ — monoclinic supergene carbonate, the Zn-dominant mirror of rosasite. Delicate pale blue-green tufted divergent sprays — high birefringence makes them shimmer under cross-polarized light. Forms in the same supergene parent fluid as rosasite (Cu + Zn + CO₃ + O₂) but precipitates only when Zn/(Cu+Zn) > 0.5; the two species are typically intergrown, separated only by ratio. Mohs 2 (scratches with a fingernail), light blue streak. Named after Plato's mythical orichalcum — the lost gold-alloy of Atlantis. Type locality: Loktevskoye Mine, Western Siberia (1839); the most aesthetic specimens come from Mapimi, Mexico. Source: research/minerals/research-aurichalcite.md (boss commit 3bfdf4a).

CaZn(AsO₄)(OH) — orthorhombic adelite-descloizite group, Ca-Zn arsenate; the direct analog of conichalcite (Ca-Cu) and mottramite (Pb-Cu-V). Hardness 4-4.5, density 4.13 g/cm³. Color colorless to pale yellow-green to bright apple-green when cuprian (toward conichalcite series — continuous solid solution per Cu/Zn substitution). Forms supergene at <60°C in Ca-buffered pore fluids with active Zn²⁺ + As(V) at pH 6.5-8.0. The cation-ratio fork from conichalcite: Cu/(Cu+Zn) < 0.5 → austinite; > 0.5 → conichalcite; sweet spot < 0.3 (pure Zn-end) with sigma multiplier 1.2. Type locality Gold Hill, Utah (Staples 1935). Substrate priority: conichalcite (epitactic) > smithsonite > dolomite. Habit dispatch: epitactic on conichalcite / hemispherical powder-puffs / acicular sprays / bladed. Looks like a paler thinner conichalcite in hand; SG ~4.1 + apple-green cuprian color when present are the field marks. Refs: research dossier 2026-05; Staples 1935 (type description); Gebhard 1999 Tsumeb pp. 155-157; Keller 1977 MinRec 8(3); Magalhães et al. 1988 (log Ksp ~–22.6 at 25°C); Handbook of Mineralogy v.IV.

Ca(UO₂)₂(PO₄)₂·11H₂O — tetragonal uranyl phosphate, the Ca-cation analog of torbernite. Bright canary-yellow tabular plates on the same {001} habit, but where torbernite's Cu²⁺ quenches the uranyl emission, autunite's Ca²⁺ does not — under longwave UV (365nm) it glows intense apple-green, one of the brightest fluorescent species known. Round 9d cation-fork mechanic: same parent fluid as torbernite (U + P + supergene-T + oxidizing), differentiated by Cu/(Cu+Ca) ratio. Ca dominates groundwater everywhere except in actively-mined Cu districts, so autunite is far more common in nature than torbernite (which gets all the museum attention). Mohs 2-2.5; dehydrates irreversibly to meta-autunite (8 H₂O) above ~80°C. Type locality: Saint-Symphorien, Autun, France (Adrien Brongniart, 1852). Sources: Pinch & Wilson 1977; research/minerals/research-uraninite.md §164-178 (paragenetic chain).

(Ni,Fe) — Ni-Fe alloy, ranging from Ni₂Fe to Ni₃Fe stoichiometry. Cubic Fm-3m, H 5, malleable, magnetic, metallic-silvery luster. THE serpentinization-driven natural metal. Forms when olivine + pyroxene of ultramafic protolith serpentinize under strongly reducing (O₂ < 0.3) and hyperalkaline (pH 9-13) conditions, releasing Ni and Fe in metallic-alloy form. Type locality AWAROA NZ 1885 (the namesake); MICROSCOPIC grains in serpentine + chrysotile matrix at most occurrences — rarely visible without microscopy. Larger nuggets at exceptional localities: Cassiar BC 1-2 mm grains; Bou Azzer Morocco; Jeffrey + Italian Alps; New Caledonia placers (secondary surface concentration). Coexists with magnetite + chrysotile + chromite in serpentinite matrix. The Ni in FluidChemistry was already added pre-v89 (speculative for millerite + annabergite + pentlandite + chrysoprase coloration); awaruite is the latest consumer. Discriminator: STRICT reducing + alkaline + S-free gate; sulfides (millerite NiS, pentlandite (Fe,Ni)9S8, heazlewoodite Ni3S2) win the Ni budget when S > 5 ppm. Refs: Anthony Handbook v.I; Bird DK & Bassett WA (1980) Fluid inclusion study of an active geothermal system Hekla Iceland (with Fe-Ni alloy stability discussion). Geochim. Cosmochim. Acta 44:1659; Krenn K & Hauzenberger CA (2007) Tonga ophiolite Fe-Ni alloy thermometry; Frost BR (1985) On the stability of sulfides, oxides and native metals in serpentinite. Contributions to Mineralogy and Petrology 91:139-153 (oxygen + sulfur fugacity controls).

Cu₃(CO₃)₂(OH)₂ — deep azure to midnight blue, the deepest blue in the common mineral kingdom. Forms in supergene oxidation zones where high pCO₂ groundwater meets Cu²⁺. Most azurite is born to become malachite: CO₂ escapes from solution over time and the higher-carbonate azurite converts to lower-carbonate malachite, preserving the original crystal shape as a green pseudomorph. Requires carbonate country rock (limestone host) for the high pCO₂ conditions.

BaSO₄, the densest non-metallic mineral collectors will encounter at 4.5 g/cm³ (the name 'barytes' from Greek βαρύς, 'heavy'). Galena's primary gangue mineral in MVT districts (Tri-State, Cumberland, Pine Point) and abundant in hydrothermal vein systems (Cavnic, Wegscheid, Sterling Hill). Acid-resistant — even concentrated H₂SO₄ won't touch it, the basis for its industrial use as drilling-mud weighting agent. Forms a partial solid solution with celestine (BaSO₄ ↔ SrSO₄); intermediates 'celestobarite' and 'barytocelestine' are common when both Ba and Sr present in the parent fluid. Famous habits: tabular 'desert rose' (Oklahoma + Saudi Arabia), bladed Cumberland fans, cockscomb cyclic twins (Romania), honey-yellow Pb-bearing variants (Cumberland gold).

PbCu₃(AsO₄)₂(OH)₂ — monoclinic Cu-ENRICHED Pb-Cu arsenate, the Cu-rich sibling of duftite. Hardness 4.5, density 5.65 g/cm³ (lighter than duftite at 6.4 — distinguishing). Color apple-green to yellow-green, grass-green, sometimes paler than duftite; rarely emerald-green. Forms supergene at <60°C where Cu activity exceeds Pb (Cu:Pb molar ~3:1) — typically near the Cu-sulfide source after Pb has been partly leached out as cerussite upstream. Type locality Penberthy Croft, Cornwall (Church 1865); Tsumeb material is more crystalline + brighter green, often as crusts on mimetite or duftite. Discriminators: vs duftite — Cu:Pb > 2.0 (above 1:1); vs olivenite — at least some Pb present (Pb ≥ 30); vs cornubite (Cu₅, no Pb) — Pb ≥ 30. Substrate priority: mimetite (provides Pb-As template, pseudomorphs documented) > duftite (epitactic, Cu-richer than substrate) > olivenite > malachite. Habit dispatch: pseudomorph_or_overgrowth / spheroidal_mammillary / botryoidal_druze / powdery_crust. Field discriminator: paler more yellow-green than duftite + lighter in hand (SG 5.7 vs 6.4) + often grungier/powdery texture (Cornwall material especially). Refs: research dossier 2026-05; Church 1865 (type description); Gebhard 1999 Tsumeb pp. 161-164; Keller 1977 MinRec 8(3); Wilson & Keller 2001 MinRec 32(3); Ghose & Wan 1979 (structure); Handbook of Mineralogy v.IV.

Be₃Al₂Si₆O₁₈ — hexagonal cyclosilicate; in this simulator's post-Round-7 architecture the beryl entry represents goshenite and the generic colorless/pale beryl that fires when no chromophore trace is above threshold. Emerald (Cr/V), morganite (Mn), heliodor (Fe+oxidizing), and aquamarine (Fe reducing/moderate) are each first-class species with their own engines. Beryllium is the most incompatible common element in magmatic systems: no rock-forming mineral takes it, so Be accumulates in residual pegmatite fluid until beryl finally nucleates at high threshold. That's why beryl crystals can be enormous — by the time the first crystal fires, there's a lot of Be waiting.

A variable, hydrous, poorly crystalline layer manganese oxide rather than a single fixed-composition MnO2 crystal. Birnessite is the scientifically appropriate first-class phase for many low-temperature stream, cave, subglacial and wet-wall manganese coatings. Potter and Rossman (1979) found stream deposits generally birnessite and cave/subglacial material resembling those stream deposits. The simulator therefore renders its booked mass as a broad nanocrystalline lining or coalesced crust, never as one trophy-sized prism. Exchangeable Na/Ca/K and water are structurally real but compositionally variable; the fixed growth ledger books Mn as the framework-limiting reagent and reports interlayer cations as traces rather than inventing an exact endmember.

Bi₂S₃ — orthorhombic bismuth sulfide, same structure as stibnite. Lead-gray to tin-white metallic, often showing yellowish/iridescent tarnish. Forms in high-T hydrothermal veins associated with arsenopyrite, chalcopyrite, cassiterite, wolframite — the tin-tungsten-arsenic greisen suite. Temperature-driven habit switch: acicular needles at T < 350°C, stout prisms at T > 350°C. When S²⁻ runs out before Bi, switches to native bismuth.

Na₂[B₄O₅(OH)₄]·8H₂O — sodium tetraborate decahydrate. The mineral that doesn’t belong in a typical hydrothermal vug: a playa-lake / closed-basin evaporite that crystallizes only from alkaline (pH > 8.5) brines rich in Na and B at low T. The defining feature is what happens after: leave a fresh borax crystal in dry air and within weeks it effloresces to white powder (tincalconite, Na₂B₄O₇·5H₂O), losing 5 of its 10 water molecules to humidity. This is the only common mineral that self-destructs in normal collection conditions — every borax specimen is a race against dehydration.

Cu₅FeS₄ — the 228°C order-disorder transition mineral. Above 228°C, Cu and Fe randomly occupy the cation sites (pseudo-cubic, high-T form); below, they order (orthorhombic). Fresh bronze-copper color on a broken surface, but the mineral tarnishes rapidly to the iridescent blue/purple/green/gold 'peacock ore' from thin-film interference on sulfide surface products. Forms both hypogene (hydrothermal, ~200–500°C) and supergene (cooler, as an enrichment mineral replacing chalcopyrite). Competes with chalcopyrite for Cu+Fe+S at different Cu:Fe ratios.

Cu₄(SO₄)(OH)₆, the wet-supergene Cu sulfate. Emerald-green prismatic crystals, distinguishable from malachite by distinctly darker green and prismatic habit (vs malachite's botryoidal). The higher-pH end (pH 4-7) of the brochantite ↔ antlerite Cu-sulfate fork — acidification (pH < 3) converts brochantite to antlerite + H₂O; alkalinization (pH > 7) converts to tenorite/malachite. Atacama Desert (Chile) supergene Cu deposits — Chuquicamata, Mansa Mina, Mantos Blancos, El Tesoro — have brochantite as a major component. Bisbee, Mt Lyell (Tasmania), Cap Garonne (France), Cananea (Mexico) all have well-known specimens. Statue of Liberty's iconic green patina is largely brochantite (chloride-rich harbor air drives the SO₄/CO₃ partition toward sulfate, not malachite).

Mg(OH)₂ — trigonal Mg hydroxide. H 2.5, density 2.39, pearly to vitreous luster, perfect {0001} cleavage producing flexible lamellae. The serpentinization byproduct mineral — when olivine + pyroxene + H₂O react to form serpentine, excess Mg precipitates as brucite. Diagnostic hyperalkaline pH (10-13), above the magnesite-carbonate stability boundary. Common at Jeffrey Mine Quebec (associated with chrysotile veining), Italian Alps Val Malenco, Marmara Turkey, Mt. Lewis NV, Wood's Mine PA (the type-locality cabinet specimens). Distinct from carbonate-substituted hydromagnesite (Mg-OH-CO3, separate mineral; brucite has no CO3). Refs: Anthony JW et al. Handbook of Mineralogy v.III; Deer Howie Zussman v.5 Non-Silicates; O'Hanley DS (1996) Serpentinites: Records of Tectonic and Petrological History. Oxford; Schramke JA, Kerrick DM, Lasaga AC (1982) Calculation of the dehydration reaction muscovite + quartz = K-feldspar + sillimanite + water (and brucite stability experiments). Geochim. Cosmochim. Acta 46:1581.

AuTe2 — the gold-telluride that broke crystallography. Goldschmidt documented 92 distinct crystal forms before the structure was even understood; the lattice carries an incommensurate modulation wave through the tellurium positions, driven by Au fluctuating between Au⁺ and Au³⁺ states. This is the structure that defied Haüy's law of rational indices for a century. Beyond the pathology, calaverite is the world's premier gold-telluride ore mineral — Cripple Creek (Colorado) and Kalgoorlie (Western Australia) are its monuments. Brass-yellow metallic luster, ~3% Ag substitution typical, photochemically stable (unlike its cousin sylvanite). Decomposes above ~450°C to native gold + Te vapor.

Retrograde solubility makes calcite the giant-maker of vugs: hotter fluid holds less Ca+CO₃, so heating precipitates calcite. Fizzes in acid. Mn²⁺ activates orange fluorescence; Fe²⁺ quenches it — the boundary between glowing and dark zones records a fluid-chemistry shift.

Pb₅Cu₂(CO₃)(SO₄)₃(OH)₆ — orthorhombic Pmcn distinctive BLUE-GREEN TO VERDIGRIS-GREEN (bluer than malachite, greener than linarite). Hardness 2.5-3, density 5.60-5.76 g/cm³. Streak greenish-white. Resinous to vitreous, slightly pearly on cleavage. Perfect {010} cleavage. Forms supergene at <60°C requiring BOTH carbonate AND sulfate in fluid (CO3:SO4 ratio ~0.3-1 sub-equimolar to equimolar; the discriminator between linarite (CO3 < 0.3) and leadhillite (CO3 > 2)). pH 5-7, sweet spot 5.5-6.5. Like linarite, needs simultaneous galena + Cu-sulfide oxidation, but with carbonate from limestone host buffering. Often forms epitactic overgrowths on linarite (parallel [001] axes) — the linarite prism core capped by caledonite tuft is the Tsumeb signature (Smith 1994 figs. p. 110-112). Type locality Leadhills, Scotland (Brooke 1820, named after Caledonia — the Latin name for Scotland). Substrate priority: linarite (epitactic — strongest preference) > anglesite > partially-oxidized galena. NON-FLUORESCENT (Cu²⁺ quench). Field discriminator: blue-GREEN (the only blue-green of the Pb-Cu sulfate trio; linarite is pure blue, leadhillite white-grey). Weak HCl fizz (carbonate present, but less than leadhillite). SG 5.6 distinguishes from malachite (4.0). Refs: research dossier 2026-05; Giacovazzo et al. 1973 Acta Cryst. B29:1986 (structure); Brooke 1820 Annals of Philosophy 16:193 (original description); Wilson & Dunn 1978 MinRec 9:251 (Leadhills); Smith 1994 Mineralogy of Tsumeb; Williams 1990 Oxide Zone Geochemistry; Handbook of Mineralogy.

K₂(UO₂)₂(VO₄)₂·3H₂O — monoclinic uranyl vanadate, the V-branch of the autunite-group anion-competition trio (with torbernite for phosphate and zeunerite for arsenate). Bright canary-yellow earthy crusts on sandstone — the mineral that paints the desert. One percent of carnotite by weight is enough to stain an entire Jurassic outcrop the color of school buses, which is how the Colorado Plateau uranium districts were prospected before instruments. Formed where oxidizing groundwater carries U⁶⁺ + V⁵⁺ + K⁺ together at the supergene front, often concentrated around organic reducing traps (petrified wood, carbonaceous shales). Mohs ~2 (soft, earthy), strongly radioactive, non-fluorescent (vanadate matrix quenches the uranyl emission). Type locality: Roc Creek, Montrose County, Colorado (1899). Sources: research/minerals/research-carnotite.md (boss commit 3bfdf4a); Colorado Plateau uranium-vanadium roll-front geology.

SnO₂ — tetragonal tin dioxide, the primary tin ore that built the Bronze Age. Sn⁴⁺ only; fully oxidized; inert under any geological conditions (melts at 1630°C, doesn't dissolve in water or acid, doesn't decompose, doesn't oxidize further — it IS the terminal weathering product). The honey-yellow to amber to chocolate-brown to black 'tinstone' that the Cornish miners called 'black jack' and the Bohemian / Saxon miners called 'Zinnstein'. Three formation environments: pegmatitic at 400-700°C (Erzgebirge, Cornwall, San Diego County) yielding prismatic dipyramids with the diagnostic ~60° elbow/knee twin on {011}; hydrothermal at 300-500°C (Bolivia tin belt, Cornish greisen veins) yielding equant blocky crystals; low-T colloidal at < 300°C yielding 'wood tin', concentric-banded botryoidal masses that survive in placer deposits. Fe (10-1000 ppm) progressively darkens; Nb/Ta couple-substitute as accessory traces. The Erzgebirge tin trade preceded the silver/bismuth/uranium eras — 'Ore Mountains' originally meant tin mountains. Sources: research/research-cassiterite.md (boss canonical 2026-05); Williamson et al. 2010 (Cornwall fluid inclusions); Förster 1992 (Erzgebirge tin geology); Anthony et al. Handbook of Mineralogy Vol. III.

SrSO₄, the strontium sulfate; isostructural with barite (the two form a partial solid solution; intermediates 'celestobarite' and 'barytocelestine' common in mixed-cation fluids). The diagnostic pale celestial blue is an F-center defect color — radiation-damaged anion vacancies absorb yellow-orange light, leaving the calm sky blue that named the species. Famous occurrences: Madagascar Sakoany geodes (football-sized, 30 cm pale-blue tabular plates — world's largest), Sicilian Caltanissetta sulfur-vug fibrous habit (radiating fibers on yellow native sulfur), Lake Erie / Put-in-Bay (Crystal Cave on South Bass Island — world's largest known geode at 35 ft³). Industrial use: source of Sr for red firework colors; ⁸⁷Sr/⁸⁶Sr-isotope tracer for paleobrine geochronology (Schwartz et al. 2018).

PbCO₃ — orthorhombic lead carbonate. Water-clear with adamantine luster and extreme birefringence (a thin slice shows doubled images). Final stable product of the lead oxidation sequence in carbonate-rich environments: galena → anglesite → cerussite. Stellate six-ray twin (cyclic twin on {110}) is among mineralogy's most iconic forms — three individuals intergrown at 120° angles producing a perfect star. Named for Latin 'cerussa' (white lead).

Ca₂Al₂Si₄O₁₂·6H₂O (chabazite-Ca, per-Ca CaAl₂Si₄O₁₂·6H₂O) — trigonal (R-3m) framework silicate, an intermediate-silica (Si/Al≈2) member of the basalt-amygdule zeolite suite. H 4-5, density 2.05-2.16 (conspicuously light), vitreous; colorless/white/flesh-pink. Very hydrous (12 H₂O per cell). The signature habit is the rhombohedral pseudo-cube — a near-90° rhombohedron that mimics a cube — plus the famous phacolite penetration twins (lens-shaped twinned aggregates, twin axis [0001]) and the Na-rich tabular herschelite. A chabazite-group SERIES (chabazite-Ca/-Na/-K/-Sr by dominant extra-framework cation, Coombs et al. 1997); the cation runs Ca > Na > K in frequency and K is NOT required — chabazite-Ca is the basalt-amygdule default. Relative paragenetic order is locality-dependent; substrate preferences do not establish chronology. Field discriminator vs CALCITE (the classic trap — the pseudo-cube rhomb looks like a calcite rhomb/cube): chabazite's {101̄1} cleavage is POOR (calcite's is perfect, three directions), it does NOT effervesce in acid, it is harder (4-5 vs 3) and notably lighter (2.1 vs 2.71); optically weakly birefringent + anomalously biaxial/sectored. Type area Sicily (Aci Castello / Cyclopean Isles, historical); famous from Bohemia (Aussig/Ústí), Nova Scotia (Wasson Bluff), the Deccan (Pune), Iceland. Refs: Passaglia & Sheppard 2001 RiMG 45:69 (crystal chemistry, R=0.67, Ca-DEC); Coombs et al. 1997 Can.Mineral. 35:1571; Akizuki & Konno 1987 Mineral.Mag. 51:427 (phacolite twinning); Calligaris et al. 1982 Zeolites (R-3m).

CuSO₄·5H₂O — the bright sky-blue water-soluble Cu sulfate, the [Cu(H₂O)₅]²⁺ chromophore one of the most intensely-colored minerals. Triclinic (P1̄), Mohs 2.5, perfect {110} cleavage. The most water-soluble mineral in the sim — re-dissolves when fluid salinity drops below 4 OR pH rises above 5 (per-step hook in VugSimulator.run_step). Geologically authentic: every chalcanthite specimen is a temporary victory over entropy. The terminal phase of the Cu-sulfate oxidation cascade (chalcopyrite → bornite → chalcocite → covellite → cuprite → brochantite → antlerite → chalcanthite). Forms in arid strongly-oxidizing very-acidic salt-concentrated drainage: Chuquicamata mine walls (Chile), Rio Tinto AMD seeps (Spain), Atacama desert evaporite crusts. Most 'natural' specimens on the market are lab-grown. Sources: research/minerals/research-chalcanthite.md (boss commit f2939da), Bandy 1938 (Am. Mineral. 23).

Cryptocrystalline, commonly fibrous SiO₂ rather than a tiny euhedral quartz habit. The simulator evaluates its own Fournier chalcedony equilibrium from 0–200°C; it can follow amorphous opal as silica activity falls and can in turn dissolve and reprecipitate as quartz. Repeated accepted microfibrous layers in basalt cavities produce an actual banded-agate fabric. Agate is therefore a recorded texture of chalcedony, not a cosmetic label for a quartz-filled vug.

Cu₂S — 79.8% Cu by weight, one of the richest copper ores. The pseudomorph thief: replaces chalcopyrite and bornite atom-by-atom in the supergene enrichment blanket, keeping the host's outline while swapping the chemistry. Forms dark gray to black metallic crystals. Pseudo-hexagonal stellate twins (cyclic sixlings on {110}) are the collector's prize. The supergene enrichment zone is where mineable copper ore gets made — weathering concentrates Cu into a layer richer than the primary sulfide above it.

CuFeS₂, the primary copper ore. Forms in porphyry systems at 200-600°C, peaking 300-500°C during K-silicate alteration. Its oxidation feeds malachite, azurite, and the whole secondary copper-carbonate paragenesis. Tarnished surfaces show iridescent 'peacock ore' colors.

FeCr2O4 — the iron-chromium spinel and the principal Cr ore. Crystallizes early from cooling mafic / ultramafic magma at 1200–1400°C, far outside the vug regime; this is fundamentally a magmatic cumulate mineral, not a hydrothermal vug phase. Listed in the spec for completeness and for placer / detrital provenance reasoning — chromite survives weathering and transport unchanged due to extreme spinel-structure stability. Bushveld (South Africa), Stillwater (Montana), Great Dyke (Zimbabwe) are the layered-intrusion type localities. Magnesiochromite (Mg → Fe substitution) and hercynite-leaning (Al → Cr substitution) are the two main solid-solution arms.

Cu₂H₂Si₂O₅(OH)₄, the cyan-blue copper silicate. Cryptocrystalline and X-ray amorphous — technically a mineraloid, though sanctioned as a mineral since 1803. Forms at 5–60 °C where meteoric groundwater carries Cu²⁺ out of a weathering copper deposit and picks up SiO₂ from silicate wall rock. At Bisbee it crusts over cuprite and native copper and famously pseudomorphs azurite once pCO₂ drops and silica floods in.

SiO2 — Ni-bearing chalcedony (microcrystalline-fibrous quartz). The apple-green chalcedony variety, colored by nano-inclusions of Ni-phyllosilicate (pimelite/willemseite/kerolite) within the silica fabric — a composite color, not a lattice color. Forms in supergene weathering of ultramafic/serpentinite protolith where olivine breaks down and meteoric groundwater scavenges Ni and silica into fractures. Mined since the 14th century at Szklary (Poland); current world reference is Marlborough (Queensland). Heat above ~150°C and prolonged sun-exposure fade the color irreversibly. Establishes the chalcedony habit family in the sim — substrate for future agate/carnelian/onyx siblings.

Mg₃Si₂O₅(OH)₄ — monoclinic serpentine-group phyllosilicate (clinochrysotile, the most common polytype; ortho- and parachrysotile are minor polytypes). H 2.5-3.5, density 2.55, silky-greasy luster, conchoidal fracture for massive form. THE asbestos of commerce — fibrous habit diagnostic with parallel-bundle silky fibers. Forms by SERPENTINIZATION: olivine + pyroxene + H₂O → serpentine minerals at T 200-500°C and pH 10-12, in ultramafic protolith (peridotite/dunite/harzburgite). Jeffrey Mine (Val-des-Sources Quebec — formerly named Asbestos QC; 1881-2011 produced ~40% of world chrysotile-asbestos; town renamed 2020). Other major producers: Thetford Mines QC, Cassiar BC, Coalinga CA, Sverdlovsk Russia, Zhetygara Kazakhstan. The asbestos health concerns (mesothelioma + asbestosis from prolonged inhalation, the 1949 Quebec Asbestos Strike etc.) are real but secondary to the geological story — at Jeffrey, the rodingite-contact cabinet assemblage is what mineral collectors value. Chrysotile is the host-matrix mineral; the rodingite minerals (vesuvianite cyprine + grossular + diopside + pectolite + datolite) crystallize within and along the chrysotile-serpentine veining. Discriminator from analogous serpentines: lizardite is platy (no fibers), antigorite is corrugated-platy (no straight fibers); chrysotile is the only true fibrous polytype. Refs: Anthony JW et al. Handbook of Mineralogy v.IIA Phyllosilicates; Deer WA, Howie RA, Zussman J Rock-Forming Minerals v.1B; Wicks FJ & Plant AG (1979) Electron-microprobe + TEM study of serpentine minerals. Canadian Mineralogist 17:785-830; O'Hanley DS (1996) Serpentinites: Records of Tectonic and Petrological History. Oxford. THE rodingite + serpentine framework. Bernardini GP (1981) MR 12(5):277.

HgS — trigonal mercury sulfide, the principal ore of mercury and the deepest cochineal red of all minerals. Nicknamed 'dragon's blood' for the pigment ancient Romans extracted from Almadén. Specific gravity 8.0-8.2 is the highest of any common ore mineral (the heft is unmistakable in hand). Decomposes at ~580°C (releases Hg vapor); destroyed by oxidation above O₂ ~1.2 (sublimes as Hg⁰ + SO₄²⁻). Type locality Almadén (Spain, mined for 2000+ years). The pigment vermillion is synthetic cinnabar.

PbSe — the selenide analog of galena. Forms in low-sulfur hydrothermal veins where Se is enriched relative to S, typically alongside other selenides (tiemannite HgSe, klockmannite Cu₂Se, naumannite Ag₂Se). Above 300°C it forms continuous solid solution with galena; below 300°C the miscibility gap opens and the two unmix into separate phases — high-T clausthalite/galena solid solutions exsolve on cooling, producing diagnostic lamellar textures. Type locality Clausthal-Zellerfeld (Harz Mountains, Germany, 1832). Important in some sandstone-type uranium deposits and in Cu-Au-U systems like Olympic Dam.

BiVO₄ — bright yellow to orange-yellow monoclinic bismuth vanadate. End of the bismuth oxidation sequence: bismuthinite → native bismuth → bismite/bismutite → clinobisvanite (if V is present). Microscopic — individual crystals rarely exceed 0.1 mm, so clinobisvanite appears as a powdery to micro-platy coating on matrix. Famously, BiVO₄ is a photocatalyst for water splitting — the same mineral that forms as a supergene afterthought is being engineered to make solar fuel. Folded into phosphate class_color (#13eb7f) per the 12-hue palette decision.

CoAsS — orthorhombic cobalt sulfarsenide (pseudo-cubic, pyritohedral habit). Tin-white with diagnostic pinkish blush from surface Co oxidation, Mohs 5.5. The cobalt analog of arsenopyrite. The three-element gate (Co + As + S all required simultaneously) makes this rare; the Cobalt-Ontario type locality is one of the few places it forms in well-developed crystals. Indian jewellers used powdered cobaltite ('sehta') to make blue enamel on gold ornaments — the source of the first Co ever isolated from a non-arsenide mineral. Sources: research/minerals/research-cobaltite.md (boss commit f2939da), Bayliss 1968 (Mineral. Mag. 36, on cobaltite-arsenopyrite substitution).

USiO₄·nH₂O — tetragonal I4₁/amd (ZIRCON-isostructural), 0 < n < ~0.25. Hardness 5-6 when crystalline (4-5 metamict); density 5.1 g/cm³ calc., 4.6-5.0 measured (hydration + metamictization lower it). Color BLACK to brownish-black to dark grey; streak dark brown to black. Brittle conchoidal fracture; metamict aggregates sectile-soft. Adamantine-greasy luster fresh, dull-earthy when oxidized. NO FLUORESCENCE — U is U⁴⁺ (lacks the uranyl UO₂²⁺ chromophore that fluoresces in U(VI) species like uranophane). PRIMARY hydrothermal mineral (not strictly supergene), forms 100-300°C in REDUCING fluids (logfO₂ < –40 at 200°C, below uraninite-haematite buffer) with aqueous SiO₂ above quartz saturation (Finch & Murakami 1999 RIMG 38:91-179 pp. 116-119). Replaces uraninite where pore-water silica activity rises (Pointer et al. 1988); also primary in roll-front sandstone-hosted U deposits. Critically, ΣCO2 must be LOW (< 10⁻³ mol/L) — high carbonate mobilizes U(IV) as uranyl-carbonate complexes and dissolves coffinite/uraninite. Phosphate < 1 ppm or ningyoite (U(IV) phosphate) competes. Type locality Cane Springs Canyon, Utah (Stieff et al. 1955 Science 121:608). Substrate priority: uraninite (replacement) > pyrite + organic matter (sandstone roll-front host) > vug wall. Refs: research dossier 2026-05; Stieff, Stern, Sherwood 1955; Finch & Murakami 1999; Burns 2005 Can. Mineral. 43:1839; Janeczek & Ewing 1992 J. Nucl. Mater. 190:157; Pointer et al. 1988 Mineralog. Mag. 52:553; Dana 7th v.IV (silicates); MinRec Schneeberg issue v.19 (1988).

CaCu(AsO₄)(OH) — orthorhombic Ca-Cu arsenate (pseudo-monoclinic via {110} twinning). Vivid emerald to apple-green from Cu²⁺ chromophore in octahedral coordination. Harder (Mohs 4.5) and brighter than its Ca-free cation analog olivenite (Mohs 3, olive-drab) — the Ca-Cu substitution stiffens the structure and shifts the absorption spectrum. Supergene mineral: forms in oxidized Cu-As vein deposits and porphyry copper oxidation zones, particularly where carbonate-buffered groundwater supplies Ca alongside the Cu and As from weathering primary sulfides/arsenides. Cation fork against olivenite — conichalcite when Ca/(Ca+Cu) > 0.4 in the local fluid; Cu-dominant routes to olivenite. The two may coexist in the same vug as a 'two-shade green' assemblage. Mn substitution possible (yellow-greenish cast). Type locality: Hinojosa de Córdoba, Spain (Breithaupt 1849). Famous from Tsumeb, Bisbee, Lavrion, Cap Garonne. Sources: research/research-conichalcite.md (boss canonical 2026-05); Anthony et al. Handbook of Mineralogy Vol. IV.

Al₂O₃ — trigonal close-packed oxide. The structural parent of ruby + sapphire, and the hardness-9 abrasive mineral (emery is Al₂O₃ + magnetite). Corundum is SiO₂-undersaturated: if any significant silica is present, Al + SiO₂ drives toward the Al₂SiO₅ polymorphs (kyanite/andalusite/sillimanite) or feldspar, not corundum. The defining constraint is SiO₂ < 50 ppm — the first upper-bound gate in this simulator. Forms in amphibolite-to-granulite-facies marble contact metamorphism (Mogok-type) and in basalt-hosted xenocrysts.

CuS — indigo-blue, the only common naturally blue mineral. Micaceous perfect basal cleavage (peels into flexible sheets like mica). Higher S:Cu ratio than chalcocite (1:1 vs 1:2), so it forms where sulfide activity is higher — at the boundary between the supergene oxidation zone and the reduced primary sulfides below. Decomposes to chalcocite + sulfur at 507°C. The name is Latin 'covellite' (for Niccolo Covelli, who discovered the Vesuvius fumarole specimens in 1833).

Na₂Fe²⁺₃Fe³⁺₂Si₈O₂₂(OH)₂ — the asbestiform variety of riebeckite, historically called "blue asbestos". Monoclinic C2/m; H about 4; density about 3.2-3.4; deep blue to lavender-blue silky fibre bundles. Important occurrences in Western Australia and the Northern Cape are hosted by metamorphosed banded iron formation. Miyano & Klein (1983) place relevant crocidolite/amosite assemblages in a 150-450°C low-to-medium-temperature family. Its relationship to tiger's-eye is scientifically disputed: Heaney & Fisher (2003) interpret synchronous antitaxial quartz-crocidolite crack-seal growth, whereas Gutzmer, Beukes & Cairncross (2004) argue that older crocidolite seams were later silicified and oxidized near the surface. The simulator exposes both models and does not present pseudomorphic replacement as settled fact.

Cu₂O — 88.8% Cu by weight. Forms at the Eh boundary between native copper (more reducing) and tenorite/malachite (more oxidizing): a narrow redox window controls its existence. Dark red to nearly black with ruby-red internal reflections (from refraction, not fluorescence). Classic habits include octahedral crystals, 'chalcotrichite' hair-like plush, and massive 'tile ore'. Often occurs with native copper and malachite in supergene Cu deposits.

CaB(SiO₄)(OH) — calcium boronosilicate (sorosilicate with B replacing Si in one tetrahedral site; Hawthorne FC, Burns PC, Grice JD 1996 Can. Min. 34:1255). Monoclinic P2₁/c, H 5-5.5, vitreous to adamantine luster, conchoidal fracture, colorless to pale-yellow / pale-pink-brown when Cu-trace, pale-yellow canary tint when Fe-trace. Low-T (50-350°C) alkaline (pH 7-12) hydrothermal vug filling in TWO distinct geological settings — both alkaline, both producing gemmy cabinet material: (1) Basaltic amygdales of the Lake Superior native-copper district (Keweenaw Peninsula MI, Isle Royale; Butler GM & Burbank WS 1929 USGS Prof. Paper 144; Bornhorst TJ 2017 GSA Memoir 213) — gemmy colorless to pale-yellow crystals with prehnite + calcite + native copper as the canonical assemblage; (2) Rodingite metasomatic contact zones in ultramafic-hosted ophiolite complexes (Jeffrey Mine, Val-des-Sources Quebec — Bernardini GP 1981 MR 12(5):277 is the canonical anchor; Val Malenco Italian Alps; New Idria CA; Coleman RG 1977 Ophiolites: Ancient Oceanic Lithosphere? Springer for the global rodingite framework) — gemmy colorless crystals with vesuvianite (often cyprine variety) + grossular + prehnite + pectolite + chrysotile gangue. The Jeffrey Mine produced the best-known cabinet datolite worldwide 1880s through mine closure 2011 — sharp gemmy crystals to several cm, often with Pectolite + Vesuvianite + Grossular associations. Anthony JW, Bideaux RA, Bladh KW, Nichols MC Handbook of Mineralogy v.IV (Arsenates, Phosphates, Vanadates) is the standard reference. Discriminator from analogous Ca-borates: datolite has Si, no other Ca-borate (colemanite, ulexite, inyoite) does. Discriminator from prehnite Ca₂Al₂Si₃O₁₀(OH)₂: prehnite has Al, datolite has B; datolite is the bonded-B borosilicate variant of the Ca-silicate family.

Pb(Zn,Cu)VO₄(OH) — orthorhombic Pb-Zn vanadate, the Zn end of the descloizite-mottramite series. Cherry-red to brown-red, Mohs 3-3.5; the Tsumeb display standard. Forms in supergene oxidation zones where Pb-Zn sulfide ore (galena + sphalerite) has weathered AND V is delivered by groundwater (red-bed roll-front signature). Cu/Zn ratio dispatch: when Cu > Zn, mottramite (the olive-green Cu sibling) takes priority instead. Sources: research/minerals/research-descloizite.md (boss commit f2939da), Strunz 1959 (Tsumeb monograph).

CaMgSi₂O₆ — monoclinic C2/c Ca-Mg endmember of the clinopyroxene group (single-chain inosilicate). H 5.5-6.5, density 3.27, vitreous luster, prismatic {100} cleavage at ~87°/93°. Forms in three settings: (1) RODINGITE METASOMATISM — Ca-Al-Mg-rich fluid from serpentinization-driven dehydration alters cross-cutting mafic dikes in ultramafic host; CHROME-DIOPSIDE (emerald green Cr-trace variety) is the Jeffrey Mine cabinet aesthetic per Bernardini 1981 MR 12(5):277; Italian Alps Val Malenco; Outokumpu Finland. (2) SKARN contact-metamorphism of dolomitic limestone (Crestmore CA, De Kalb NY, Pakistan, the Roopnarine 2017 review covers North American skarns); the white-grey colorless form dominates. (3) KIMBERLITE / PERIDOTITE XENOLITHS — gem-quality chrome-diopside in mantle-derived rocks (Tanzania Mahenge, Russia Yakutia Mir mine, Outokumpu shield-derived). Trace-cation color dispatch: Cr > 0.5 ppm → chrome-diopside emerald-green (Cr³⁺ in M2 site, d-d transitions at 14500 + 22500 cm⁻¹); Fe > 20 ppm → grey-green-brown (the common skarn shade); pure → colorless/white. Refs: Anthony Handbook v.IIB Single-Chain Silicates; Deer Howie Zussman v.2A; Cameron M & Papike JJ (1981) 'Structural and chemical variations in pyroxenes', Reviews in Mineralogy 7:5-92; Bernardini GP (1981) MR 12(5):277 Jeffrey canonical; Manning 1968 Am. Min. 53:1187 (chrome-diopside crystal field).

CuSiO₃·H₂O — emerald-green trigonal cyclosilicate (six-membered Si₆O₁₈ rings linked by Cu²⁺), the Tsumeb 2nd-oxidation-zone signature mineral. Type locality Altyn-Tyube, Kazakhstan (Hauy 1797). Hardness 5, density 3.31 g/cm³, perfect rhombohedral {1011} cleavage (the property that named the mineral — Greek dia+optazein, 'to see through'). Forms supergene at 25-120°C in mildly alkaline (pH 6.5-8.0) oxidizing pore fluids where carbonate has been LOCALLY EXHAUSTED by prior malachite/azurite precipitation, leaving Cu-Si-rich residual water. The HCO₃ gate is the discriminator from malachite — same Cu source, different anion availability. Cl > 5000 ppm suppresses (CuCl complexes keep Cu mobile). Two textbook generations at Tsumeb (Keller 1977): pre-calcite needles and post-calcite gemmy prisms. Field discriminator vs. emerald: softer (H 5 vs. 7.5-8), denser (3.3 vs. 2.7), strong rhombohedral cleavage, much higher birefringence (visible doubling of back facets in a 5 mm crystal). Refs: research dossier 2026-05; Ribbe/Gibbs/Hamil 1977 Am. Min. 62:807 (structure); Keller 1977 MinRec 8(3) (Tsumeb paragenesis); Lombaard et al. 1986 (Tsumeb monograph); Anthony et al. Handbook of Mineralogy v.II.

CaMg(CO₃)₂ — the ordered double carbonate, with Ca and Mg in alternating cation layers (R3̄ space group, distinct from calcite's R3̄c). Rarely forms at surface temperature ('dolomite problem' in geology — modern oceans should but don't precipitate it for kinetic reasons). Above 50°C with both Ca and Mg present in roughly comparable amounts (Mg/Ca ratio 0.3-5, optimum 1:1), dolomite competes with calcite (low Mg) and theoretical magnesite (no Ca, not modeled). The host rock of MVT deposits and a major sedimentary carbonate. Saddle-shaped curved rhombohedra are the diagnostic habit — the lattice strain from cation ordering shows in the surface geometry.

PbCu(AsO₄)(OH) — orthorhombic ADELITE-DESCLOIZITE group, Pb-Cu analog of conichalcite (Ca-Cu) and mottramite (Pb-Cu vanadate). Hardness 3, density 6.40 g/cm³ (HEAVY — Pb is diagnostic in hand). Color olive-green to grass-green to grey-green, sometimes apple-green. Forms supergene at <60°C from Pb + Cu + As(V) in carbonate-buffered fluid at pH 5.5-7.5. Discriminator from bayldonite (the Cu-enriched sibling): duftite at Pb:Cu near 1:1 in fluid (Cu:Pb < 2.0); bayldonite at Pb:Cu near 1:3 (Cu:Pb > 2.0). Discriminator from mottramite: As vs V in fluid — duftite if As(V) > V; mottramite if V > As. One of the MOST COMMON Tsumeb arsenates, occurring on nearly every Pb-Cu oxide assemblage. Substrate priority: malachite > cerussite > mimetite > azurite. Pseudomorphs after azurite and mimetite documented. Habit dispatch: botryoidal crust (textbook) / spheroidal / mammillary / drusy. Field discriminator: olive-drab green + very heavy in hand (SG 6.4) + no carbonate fizz vs azurite. Refs: research dossier 2026-05; Pufahl 1920 (type description, Tsumeb); Gebhard 1999 Tsumeb pp. 173-177; Keller 1977 MinRec 8(3); Wilson & Keller 2001 MinRec 32(3); Kharisun et al. 1998 Mineralog. Mag. 62 (structure); Handbook of Mineralogy v.II.

Be₃Al₂Si₆O₁₈ with Cr³⁺ (or V³⁺) substituting for Al — the green variety of beryl. The 'emerald paradox': Cr is commonly supplied by mafic-ultramafic or Cr-bearing sedimentary rocks while Be is commonly pegmatitic; the required chemistries rarely coexist. Classic deposits include Colombia's black-shale-hosted systems and Zambia's schist-hosted Kagem district. Ordinary green beryl is not automatically emerald without the required chromophore and gemological evidence.

Cu₃AsS₄ — orthorhombic high-sulfidation Cu-As-S sulfosalt, the primary Cu mineral at Butte MT, Chuquicamata Chile, Bisbee AZ (Sacramento-Lavender Pit), Tsumeb upper sulfide zone, Lepanto Philippines, El Indio Chile, Goldfield NV, Quiruvilca Peru. Hardness 3, density 4.46 g/cm³, perfect {110} prismatic cleavage (THE field discriminator from tennantite — tennantite has no cleavage). Steel-gray to iron-black with bright metallic luster on fresh fracture; tarnishes dull. Diagnostic 60° twin on {320} produces pseudo-hexagonal trilling outlines. The defining environment is HIGH-SULFIDATION: acidic (pH 1-3), advanced argillic alteration assemblage (pyrophyllite, alunite, kaolinite, dickite, native sulfur) where SO₂ disproportionation drives both the acidity and the high f(S₂). Below ~320°C the same composition forms luzonite (tetragonal I-42m) — they're polymorphs, not a solid-solution series. The simulator engine fires the same supersaturation logic across the full T range but flags the polymorph for narrative. Supergene oxidation releases a large As budget (the AMD As-load signature of Butte/Bisbee/Chuquicamata) plus brochantite + cuprite + chalcocite + scorodite. Field discriminator from tennantite: metallic luster + perfect prismatic cleavage + striations + darker color + larger crystals; tennantite is submetallic, no cleavage, equant tetrahedral crystals, with cherry-red thin-edge transmission. Refs: research dossier 2026-05; Einaudi/Hedenquist/Inan 2003 SEG SP10:285-313 (the canonical f(S₂)-T sulfidation diagram); Sack & Loucks 1985 Am. Min. 70:1270-1289; Brimhall 1979,1980 (Butte paragenesis); Posfai & Buseck 1998 (enargite/luzonite phase relations); Anthony et al. Handbook of Mineralogy.

Ca₂(Al,Fe³⁺)₃(SiO₄)(Si₂O₇)O(OH) — monoclinic (P2₁/m) sorosilicate, the Fe³⁺ endmember of the clinozoisite–epidote series (epidote sensu stricto = Fe³⁺ ≥ 0.5 apfu at the M3 site, Armbruster et al. 2006 EJM 18:551). H 6-7, density 3.38-3.49, vitreous luster, perfect {001} cleavage, strong pleochroism, the diagnostic PISTACHIO-GREEN from Fe³⁺ (the green deepens with pistacite content). The classic ALPINE-CLEFT / greenschist-facies mineral: lustrous prisms striated ∥b in low-salinity oxidized metamorphic fissures. World-best gem prisms from Tormiq Valley (Haramosh Mts., Gilgit-Baltistan, Pakistan — named type-quality in the Handbook of Mineralogy, rivaling Knappenwand, Austria). THE LOAD-BEARING CONTROL IS REDOX: epidote requires ferric iron, so an OXIDIZING fluid near the hematite-magnetite buffer; under reducing conditions Fe partitions into magnetite + actinolite (Fe²⁺) and clinozoisite forms instead of green epidote (Holdaway 1972 CMP 37:307; Liou 1973 J.Petrol 14:381). Discriminator from catalog cousins: vs actinolite (amphibole, Mg + Fe²⁺, cleavage 56°/124°); vs prehnite (botryoidal, no striated prisms); vs diopside (pyroxene, 87°/93° cleavage); vs grossular (isometric, isotropic); vs vesuvianite (tetragonal, weak birefringence). Refs: Anthony et al. Handbook of Mineralogy 2001 (epidote sheet, names Tormiq); Deer Howie Zussman Rock-Forming Minerals v.1B (1986) pp.44-134; Liebscher & Franz eds. 2004 Reviews in Mineralogy v.56 Epidotes; Armbruster et al. 2006 EJM 18:551 (nomenclature).

Co₃(AsO₄)₂·8H₂O — the crimson-pink 'cobalt bloom' of medieval miners. A low-T supergene arsenate formed by oxidation of primary cobalt arsenides (cobaltite, skutterudite). Shares the vivianite-group structure with annabergite (Ni), and forms a continuous solid solution: Ni substitution for Co pales the color from crimson-pink through purplish-pink toward apple-green. Dehydrates above 200°C.

Potassium feldspar — the most abundant mineral in Earth's crust. The polymorph records T: sanidine (>500°C) → orthoclase (300-500°C) → microcline (<300°C, with diagnostic cross-hatched twinning). Pb substitution for K creates amazonite, the green pegmatite feldspar.

Fe₂(MoO₄)₃·nH₂O, the no-lead branch of Mo oxidation. Canary-yellow acicular tufts to powdery crusts on molybdenite surfaces. Fast-growing, powdery, hardness ~2. Coexists with wulfenite (both draw on oxidized MoO₄²⁻) but wins the early window. Geologically more common than wulfenite; under-represented in collections because it's yellow fuzz, not display material. Type locality Climax (Colorado); abundant in any porphyry Cu-Mo oxidation zone.

CaF₂, a cubic halide with retrograde solubility. Classic MVT companion to sphalerite and galena. The word 'fluorescent' derives from fluorite — blue-violet under both LW and SW UV, driven by REE substitution and radiation-damage color centers.

PbS, the densest common sulfide (SG 7.6). Perfect cubic cleavage — tap it and it shatters into tiny cubes. Argentiferous galena was the historic source of most of the world's silver: Potosí, Leadville, Broken Hill.

FeO(OH), rust with a crystal name. Low-T oxidation product of Fe-sulfides and Fe²⁺ fluids. Velvety-black botryoidal surfaces and the classic boxwork pseudomorph after pyrite — the Egyptian Prophecy Stones are goethite after marcasite. Dehydrates to hematite above 300°C.

CdS — the hexagonal (wurtzite-structure) cadmium sulfide. The 'cadmium yellow' pigment, mineral form. Forms by supergene oxidation of Cd-bearing sphalerite: Cd substitutes for Zn in primary sphalerite up to ~1%, gets liberated when sphalerite oxidizes, and re-precipitates as CdS when Cd²⁺ encounters residual sulfide in the supergene zone. Ksp ~10⁻²⁸ — extreme insolubility means trace Cd precipitates readily. Hemimorphic crystals (different terminations at top vs. bottom) are diagnostic. Type locality Bishopton, Scotland (1840 railway tunnel cut). Tsumeb (Namibia) is the modern reference. Hexagonal greenockite is the high-T polymorph (>200°C); cubic hawleyite is the low-T form.

Ca₃Al₂(SiO₄)₃ — cubic Ia-3d Ca-Al endmember of the garnet group (orthosilicate). H 6.5-7.5, density 3.59, vitreous to adamantine luster, no cleavage, conchoidal fracture. Forms in three settings: (1) RODINGITE METASOMATISM — Ca-Al-rich fluid from serpentinization-driven dehydration alters cross-cutting mafic dikes in ultramafic host (Jeffrey Mine Quebec — Bernardini 1981 MR 12(5):277 documents chromian green + hessonite varieties; Asbestos Hill NL; Italian Alps Val d'Ala IS the type-locality for HESSONITE; Outokumpu Finland). (2) SKARN contact-metamorphism of impure limestone (Vesuvius IT type 1795 area; Crestmore CA chromian variety; Sierra de Cruces MX hessonite; De Kalb NY). (3) Carbonatite alteration (rare; late-magmatic; Kovdor RU). VARIETIES via trace-cation dispatch (no new field needed — reads existing FluidChemistry Cr/Mn/Fe): chromian green (Cr trace > 1 ppm, sometimes called 'tsavorite sensu lato' though strict tsavorite is the Tsavo East National Park material; Cr³⁺ d-d transitions), hessonite (orange-pink — Mn²⁺ + Fe³⁺ crystal-field combination per Manning JE 1967 Min. Mag. 36:572 + Geiger CA 2004 RIMG 56:213), leuco-hessonite intermediate (Fe trace), colorless/pale-yellow pure (rare; Jeffrey best material). Discriminator from analogous garnets: ANDRADITE Ca₃Fe₂(SiO₄)₃ (Fe replaces Al — would route via separate Andradite engine when wired); SPESSARTINE Mn₃Al₂(SiO₄)₃ (Mn replaces Ca — separate engine); UVAROVITE Ca₃Cr₂(SiO₄)₃ (Cr replaces Al — high-Cr endmember, rare). The chromian-grossular variety encoded HERE is Cr substituting trace in Al-rich grossular, NOT the uvarovite endmember. References: Anthony JW et al. Handbook of Mineralogy v.IA Orthosilicates; Deer WA, Howie RA, Zussman J Rock-Forming Minerals v.1A; Manning & Bird 1990 J. Petrol. 31:1; Bernardini GP 1981 MR 12(5):277; Manning 1967 Min. Mag. 36:572; Geiger 2004 RIMG 56:213; Werner AG 1797 ('granat' nomenclature).

CaHAsO₄·H₂O — orthorhombic hydrated calcium arsenate, the half-dehydrated cousin of pharmacolite. Forms EXCLUSIVELY as a transformation product of pharmacolite (CaHAsO₄·2H₂O) — heat above ~80°C OR sustained dry-air exposure drives off 1 of the 2 H₂O molecules, collapsing the lattice from monoclinic pharmacolite to orthorhombic haidingerite. The transformation is irreversible (re-humidifying does not restore the pharmacolite hydrate). External crystal shape is preserved through the in-situ transformation: a haidingerite specimen IS a former pharmacolite crystal, frozen mid-decay. Specific gravity rises from pharmacolite's 2.64-2.73 to haidingerite's 2.85-2.96 — the diagnostic water-loss densification signature. Colorless to white, vitreous luster with pearly cleavage faces on {010}. Mohs 2-2.5 (same as pharmacolite). Sectile tenacity: thin laminae are slightly flexible (unlike pharmacolite which is brittle); a useful field discriminator. Sub-millimeter crystals (Handbook of Mineralogy notes 'to 1 mm'); typically encountered as botryoidal or fibrous coatings on weathered arsenide vein assemblages. Type locality Jáchymov (Joachimsthal), Czech Republic. Named for Wilhelm Karl von Haidinger (1795-1871), Austrian mineralogist. Type pseudomorph occurrence: Getchell mine, Nevada (Handbook of Mineralogy: 'Formed by dehydration of pharmacolite (Getchell mine, Nevada, USA)'). Sources: Palache, Berman, Frondel 1951 (Dana's System of Mineralogy 7th ed v.II 708-709); Ferraris, Jones, Yerkess 1972 (Acta Cryst. 28:209-214, neutron + X-ray structure refinement); Cassien, Herpin, Permingeat 1966 (Bull. Minéral. 89:18-22, crystal structure paper).

NaCl, rock salt — the canonical chloride evaporite. Forms by evaporative concentration of Na-Cl-rich brines: closed-basin playas, sabkha, drained vugs in the supergene zone. Hopper-growth (skeletal cube with pyramidal hollows) is the signature high-supersaturation habit; clean cubes form when the brine concentrates slowly. Type localities: Wieliczka Salt Mine (Poland — meter-scale cubes, the cathedral carved in salt); Stassfurt (Germany — brilliant blue irradiated halite); Searles Lake (California — pink hoppered crystals from evaporation ponds with halobacterial carotenoids).

CdS — the cubic (sphalerite-structure) polymorph of greenockite. Identical chemistry, different lattice. Hawleyite is the kinetically favored form at low T (<100°C); it is thermodynamically metastable relative to hexagonal greenockite but persists indefinitely once formed. Always microcrystalline — no specimen anywhere has shown a discrete crystal. Bright cadmium yellow powdery coatings on sphalerite, siderite, galena in oxidation zones. Indistinguishable from greenockite by sight; XRD is the only test. Type locality Hector-Calumet mine, Yukon (1955). Most 'greenockite' in old collections is probably hawleyite.

Be₃Al₂Si₆O₁₈ with Fe³⁺ (oxidized) — the yellow variety of beryl. Same Fe cation as aquamarine but in the 3+ oxidation state; the aquamarine/heliodor split is the cleanest redox record in the gem world. Volodarsk (Namibia) is the type locality for deep-yellow 'Namibian heliodor'; Urals (Russia) and Minas Gerais (Brazil) also produce.

Fe₂O₃, the ferric iron oxide. Habit changes with T: specular-platy above 300°C, botryoidal kidney-ore below 150°C, earthy red-ochre at surface. The rosette iron-rose is a metamorphic-hydrothermal classic from the Swiss Alps.

Zn₄Si₂O₇(OH)₂·H₂O — orthorhombic SOROSILICATE, space group Imm2 (POLAR — the hemimorphic class, the textbook example of polar crystal symmetry: c-axis terminates differently top vs. bottom). Hardness 4.5-5, density 3.40-3.50 g/cm³. Color colorless to white to pale blue-green (Mapimi blue is from minor Cu²⁺); silky-vitreous on fibrous aggregates, pearly on cleavage. Forms STRICTLY supergene at <50°C in Zn-supergene zones with SiO₂ ≥ 200 ppm and CO₃ < SiO₂ (otherwise smithsonite wins). pH 5.5-8, sweet spot 6.0-7.5. The CO₃:SiO₂ ratio is the fork from smithsonite (smithsonite > 1, hemimorphite < 1). Above ~250°C dehydrates to willemite + quartz. PYROELECTRIC + piezoelectric — historical name source (Greek hemi-morphos, half-form). Type localities Tsumeb (world reference fan sheaves), Mapimi/Ojuela Mexico (blue botryoidal), Bisbee, Sterling Hill NJ, Wenshan Yunnan, Trepca Kosovo. Late in supergene Zn oxidation — post-smithsonite (Boni & Mondillo 2015 fig. 4). Substrate priority: smithsonite (epitactic, similar Zn-O coordination) > Fe-Mn gossan > relict sphalerite (in-situ replacement). Field discriminator: hemimorphic terminations diagnostic when visible; pyroelectric test (warm crystal picks up dust on one end). Distinguishes from prehnite (denser, hemimorphic vs. centrosymmetric). Refs: research dossier 2026-05; Hitzman et al. 2003 Econ. Geol. 98:685-714 (esp. fig. 9 silica-carbonate stability); Boni & Mondillo 2015 Ore Geol. Rev. 67:208-233; Takahashi 1960 Econ. Geol. 55:1084; Dana 7th v.II p.508; Handbook of Mineralogy v.II.

Ag2Te — the silver-telluride end-member of the silver chalcogenide family. Forms in low-sulfidation epithermal veins where Te is enriched and S is suppressed; wins over acanthite (Ag2S) only when S²⁻ is locally depleted. Phase transition at 155°C (cubic ↔ monoclinic) leaves diagnostic lamellar textures in slow-cooled specimens — a game-readable thermometer. Cripple Creek (Colorado), Sacarîmb (Romania), Kalgoorlie (Western Australia) are the type telluride districts. Often a major silver carrier in epithermal Au-Ag deposits. Forms a continuous spectrum with naumannite (Ag2Se) where Se substitutes for Te.

(Ca,Na)Al₂Si₇O₁₈·6H₂O (heulandite-Ca) — monoclinic (C2/m) framework silicate of the zeolite group. H 3.5-4, density 2.10-2.20, vitreous, pearly on {010}; colourless/white/grey or red-orange when Fe-stained (the classic Berufjord, Iceland and Deccan look). The WARMER, dehydrated member of the stilbite/heulandite couple — the dehydration product of stilbite (Ca-stilbite = Ca-heulandite + H₂O, Kiseleva Navrotsky Belitsky & Fursenko 2001) — so it forms at higher silica activity and the warmer end of the zeolite window. Signature habit is the 'coffin-shaped' tablet parallel to {010}, widest at the centre (Handbook of Mineralogy). The heulandite/clinoptilolite boundary is COMPOSITIONAL: Si/Al < 4.0 = heulandite, ≥ 4.0 = clinoptilolite (Coombs et al. 1997) — clinoptilolite is not modelled here, and the boundary is not a hard fluid gate because the sim's SiO2 ppm is dissolved silica, not framework Si/Al. Deccan Traps amygdule Stage-II classic (Nashik, Poona, Bombay — the Handbook lists large Deccan crystals) on a chalcedony/quartz veneer with stilbite, apophyllite, scolecite, mesolite and calcite. Field discriminator: heulandite = isolated coffin tablets; stilbite = sheaves/bowties; clinoptilolite needs Si/Al ≥ 4 + is far more thermally stable. Refs: Anthony et al. Handbook of Mineralogy (formula, cell, twin {100}); Coombs et al. 1997 Can. Mineral. 35:1571 (Si/Al=4.0 boundary); Kiseleva Navrotsky Belitsky & Fursenko 2001 Am. Mineral. 86:448; Ottens et al. 2019 (Deccan).

Ca(1-x)Mg(x)CO3 with x ≈ 0.05-0.30 — disordered Mg-substituted calcite. The kinetic precursor to ordered dolomite per the Kim et al. 2023 cyclic-Ω ordering mechanism. Forms as microcrystalline cement in modern marine, sabkha, and warm-shallow settings (Persian Gulf intertidal cements, Florida Bay Holocene marine cements, hot-spring tufas), and as biogenic skeletal material in echinoderms, coralline algae, foraminifera, and bryozoans (where biogenic-mediated x reaches 12-30 mol% Mg, occasionally up to 45% in red coralline algae per Stanley et al. 2002). Not an IMA species — varietal-name on the calcite-dolomite solid solution; above x ≈ 0.45 structure tilts irreversibly toward dolomite. Same R3̄c rhombohedral lattice as calcite; distinguishable only by XRD d104 peak shift (Goldsmith & Graf 1958 Am. Mineral. 43:84) — the d104 spacing decreases linearly with mol% Mg. Mohs hardness 3 (calcite-like; Mg substitution stiffens marginally). Color gray-to-white, with biogenic varieties picking up organic-pigment browns. Solubility ~0.1 log Ksp higher than calcite per mol% Mg (Bischoff, Mackenzie & Bishop 1987 GCA 51:1413). Discrete cabinet-scale HMC crystals are very rare — most occurrences are cement or skeletal phase. Diagenesis: HMC → LMC (low-Mg calcite) via Mg leaching over geological time without cycling; HMC → ordered dolomite under cyclic-Ω modulation per Kim 2023.

Zn₅(CO₃)₂(OH)₆ — monoclinic C2/m carbonate-hydroxide. Hardness 2-2.5 (soft — fingernail-scratchable, diagnostic), density 3.5-4.0 g/cm³ (variable with porosity). Color CHALK-WHITE to creamy white, occasionally pale yellow or pink (trace Cd or Co). Forms strictly low-T (<30°C) in alkaline (pH 7.5-9) supergene Zn zones with high CO₃ and LOW SiO₂ (<50 — otherwise hemimorphite wins). Suppressed by Cu (Cu/(Cu+Zn) < 0.15, otherwise aurichalcite wins the Zn-Cu carbonate-hydroxide solid solution). The LATEST + COOLEST member of the Zn supergene suite (Hitzman 2003 fig. 4). Wet-dry cycling (humid + evaporative seasons) produces the textbook cave-floor coatings. Type locality Iglesiente, Sardinia (Naracauli + Monteponi); also Mežica Slovenia (rare crystals), Tsumeb (minor on smithsonite), Broken Hill NSW. The Naracauli cyanobacteria-mediated biofilm hydrozincite (Preisig et al. 2014) is independently important as a natural bioremediator of Zn-contaminated drainage. Field discriminator: pale-blue SW-UV fluorescence (DEFECT-related, not Mn²⁺ activator like willemite); H 2 (scratches with fingernail, distinguishing from smithsonite H=5); SG 3.5-4 lighter than smithsonite (4.4-4.5). Often mistaken for calcite efflorescence at hand-specimen scale — UV resolves it. Refs: research dossier 2026-05; Hitzman et al. 2003 (Table 2 supergene Zn stabilities); Boni & Mondillo 2015 (Iglesiente + Naracauli sections); Preisig et al. 2014 (biofilm Naracauli); Ghaderi et al. 1999 (Mežica crystals); Dana 7th v.II p.252; Handbook of Mineralogy v.II.

KFe³⁺₃(SO₄)₂(OH)₆, the diagnostic acid-mine-drainage mineral. Yellow-to-ocher pseudocubic rhombs and powdery crusts; the supergene Fe-sulfate that takes over from goethite when pH drops below 4. Confirmed on Mars at Meridiani Planum by NASA's MER Opportunity Mössbauer spectrometer in 2004 (Klingelhöfer et al. 2004) — the first confirmation of past liquid water + acidic conditions on Mars. Earth localities: Rio Tinto (Spain — the Phoenician + Roman + Spanish + Rio Tinto Co. mining district that names the red-orange river), Red Mountain Pass (Colorado), Mojave acid drainage sites, every active sulfide-mine tailings pond. Above pH 4 dissolves and the released Fe³⁺ goes to goethite — the diagnostic AMD weathering succession.

Zn₃(AsO₄)₂·8H₂O — monoclinic VIVIANITE-GROUP, Zn end-member (series with erythrite Co, annabergite Ni, hörnesite Mg, parasymplesite Fe²⁺). Hardness 2.5-3 (soft — fingernail-scratchable, diagnostic), density 3.33 g/cm³. Color pale rose-pink (cobaltian-zinc-tinge), carmine-red (with erythrite component), peach, pale lilac, or near-colorless when pure Zn; pure Zn end-member is white to very pale pink. Perfect {010} cleavage (vivianite-group signature). Forms strictly supergene at <35°C in strongly acidic (pH < 3), damp Zn-rich oxidation pockets — the 8 H₂O is fragile, dehydrating rapidly above 50°C. Discriminator from erythrite/annabergite: the bounded solution-chemistry proxy requires Zn to exceed half of the molar dissolved Zn+Co+Ni cation pool and Ni to remain at or below 5 mol%; it does not claim to predict crystal-site occupancy without fluid–solid partition coefficients. Co substitution is extensive, while significant köttigite–Ni substitution is not supported by Ciesielczuk et al. Substrate priority: erythrite > annabergite (epitactic — same structure) > smithsonite. Type locality Schneeberg, Saxony (Daubrée 1850); at Tsumeb it is reported from the deep third oxidation zone zinc pocket, not the first-stage gossan. Field discriminator: pink-to-colorless soft (H 2.5-3) bladed crystals with perfect one-direction cleavage = vivianite-group; SG 3.3 lighter than austinite (4.1) or adamite (4.4). Refs: Ciesielczuk et al. 2020, doi:10.3390/min10060548; Hill 1979; Bowell 2014; Magalhães et al. 1988; Handbook of Mineralogy v.IV.

Pb₄(SO₄)(CO₃)₂(OH)₂ — monoclinic P2₁/a, PSEUDO-TRIGONAL (the pseudo-symmetry produces characteristic HEXAGONAL-LOOKING tablets but true symmetry is monoclinic). Hardness 2.5, density 6.55 g/cm³ (VERY heavy, distinctive in hand). Color colorless to white to pale yellow/green/grey; the pearly luster on {001} gives a milky appearance. Streak white. PERFECT {001} cleavage — peels in pearly sheets like mica. Polysynthetic twinning visible as striations on basal plates. Two polymorphs: leadhillite (monoclinic, common ambient) + susannite (trigonal P-3, higher-T variant); inversion near 80°C, reversible. METASTABLE at ambient — slowly transforms to anglesite + cerussite under humidity cycling (Pollard et al. 1992 Mineralog. Mag. 56:359). Museum specimens degrade over decades unless kept dry. Forms supergene at <60°C with mixed carbonate + sulfate; CO3:SO4 ratio > 2 (Mereiter, Völlenkle & Preisinger 1979 TMPM 26:79). pH 6-8, sweet spot 6.5-7.5 — the most alkaline of the trio. Cu must be LOW (< 50 ppm) — Cu inclusion drives to caledonite or linarite. Typical setting: galena oxidation in carbonate-host (limestone, dolostone) with well-buffered groundwater. Type locality Leadhills, Scotland (Beudant 1832; Wilson & Dunn 1978). Substrate priority: cerussite (epitactic) > anglesite > galena. NON-FLUORESCENT (Pb²⁺ quench; some specimens show weak yellow-orange SW UV from trace Mn²⁺, not diagnostic). Field discriminator: pearly white-grey tablets with mica-like cleavage + extremely high density (6.5+) + fizz weakly with WARM dilute HCl. The 'hexagonal-tablet but really monoclinic' habit is unmistakable. Refs: research dossier 2026-05; Steele et al. 1998 Mineralog. Mag. 62:451 (structure + polymorphism); Mereiter et al. 1979 TMPM 26:79; Pollard et al. 1992 Mineralog. Mag. 56:359 (alteration); Smith 1994 Mineralogy of Tsumeb; Wilson & Dunn 1978 MinRec 9:251 (Leadhills); Dana 7th v.II; Handbook of Mineralogy.

Zn₂(AsO₄)(OH)·H₂O — monoclinic hydrated Zn arsenate, BRIGHT CANARY-YELLOW (the diagnostic Tsumeb color). Hardness 4.5-5, density 4.01 g/cm³. Vitreous-brilliant luster, almost adamantine on prism faces; brittle, fragile acicular crystals snap easily. Forms supergene at <50°C in mildly acidic (pH 4.5-6.5) Zn-rich Ca-poor pore fluids — distinguishes from austinite (pH 6.5-8, Ca-Zn co-present) by the Ca-FREE + acidic condition. The structural H₂O makes it sensitive to dehydration above ~120°C. Type locality Flor de Peña mine, Nuevo León, Mexico (Drugman & Hey 1932), but TSUMEB IS UNRIVALED in size + color — the 25 cm 'Aztec sun' specimen (Smithsonian) is canonical. Substrate priority: adamite (most common — same Zn-As chemistry) > willemite > limonite-coated dolomite. Habit dispatch: Aztec-sun radiating sprays / wedge-prismatic / on adamite / solitary. Field discriminator: UNMISTAKABLE — bright canary yellow + acicular wedge habit + brilliant vitreous luster. No other Tsumeb arsenate has that color and habit combination. Refs: research dossier 2026-05; Drugman & Hey 1932 Mineralog. Mag. 23:175; Gebhard 1999 Tsumeb pp. 197-202; Keller 1977 MinRec 8(3); Wilson & Keller 2001 MinRec 32(3); Handbook of Mineralogy.

γ-FeOOH — the ruby-red hydroxide dimorph of goethite. Same formula, different crystal structure: goethite is a 3D framework (yellow-brown needles), lepidocrocite is layered (ruby-red micaceous plates). Particle size controls the hue — nanoscale plates appear pink to mauve, coarser crystals rust-red. Kinetically favored over goethite under RAPID oxidation of Fe²⁺ (e.g., pyrite weathering in situ); slow oxidation gives goethite instead. Transforms to goethite over geological time or to maghemite/hematite when heated. 'Lithium quartz' sold in rock shops is actually nanoscale lepidocrocite included in quartz.

K(Li,Al)₃(Al,Si)₄O₁₀(F,OH)₂ — monoclinic trioctahedral lithium mica, the polylithionite-trilithionite solid-solution series. Perfect {001} cleavage produces paper-thin flexible sheets (inelastic, unlike muscovite). The diagnostic pink-to-purple color comes from Mn²⁺ in the octahedral sites — Evans & Raftery 1982 settled this; trace lithium does not produce the color, despite folk-mineralogy claims. Late-pegmatite mineral: forms when residual fluid is enriched in Li + F + K simultaneously, AFTER spodumene + early micas have nucleated. Often replaces spodumene during late hydrothermal alteration (the documented Brazil/Maine paragenesis). Maximum size 20 cm books (Himalaya Mine, San Diego County); typical 1-10 mm scaly aggregates in vugs. THERMOLUMINESCENT — 50-200°C heating releases visible light from trapped defect charge carriers (no activator ion required). The Rožná pegmatite was where Bunsen & Kirchhoff extracted 150 kg of lepidolite in 1861 to isolate rubidium. Source: research/research-lepidolite.md (boss canonical 2026-05).

PbCu(SO₄)(OH)₂ — monoclinic P2₁/m DEEP AZURE TO ULTRAMARINE BLUE (some authors call it the most intensely blue mineral known). Hardness 2.5, density 5.30-5.35 g/cm³ (HEAVY — Pb is diagnostic in hand). Streak pale blue. Adamantine to vitreous, subadamantine on cleavages. Perfect {100} cleavage with {001} interrupted — prisms split lengthwise. Forms strictly supergene at <60°C requiring SIMULTANEOUS oxidation of galena AND a Cu-sulfide (chalcocite/covellite/chalcopyrite) in close proximity (mm to cm). pH 4-7, sweet spot 5-6. ΣCO2 must be LOW (< 10⁻⁴ mol/L, < 6 ppm HCO3⁻; CO3:SO4 < 0.3 in fluid) — any carbonate diverts to caledonite/leadhillite. Cl < 100 ppm (otherwise boleite group wins). Often mistaken for azurite (same color range) but linarite is HEAVIER (5.3 vs 3.8), has NO HCl fizz (sulfate-hydroxide vs carbonate), sits directly on galena (azurite never directly on galena). Type locality Leadhills-Wanlockhead Scotland (Wilson & Dunn 1978 MinRec 9:251). Mid-to-late supergene Pb-Cu oxidation cycle. Substrate priority: galena (primary substrate, with anglesite rind) > anglesite > chalcocite > cerussite. NON-FLUORESCENT (Pb²⁺ + Cu²⁺ quench). Refs: research dossier 2026-05; Effenberger 1987 N. Jb. Mineral. Mh. (structure); Smith 1994 'Mineralogy of Tsumeb'; Wilson & Dunn 1978; Williams 1990 'Oxide Zone Geochemistry'; Graeme 1981 MinRec 12:258 (Bisbee); Dana 7th v.II; Handbook of Mineralogy.

FeAs₂ — orthorhombic Pnnm (löllingite group — the namesake). Hardness 5-5.5 (Mohs) but VHN 859-920 — HIGHEST microhardness of the quartet despite lowest Mohs (characteristic of marcasite-group structure). Density 7.40-7.47 g/cm³. Color STEEL-GRAY TO SILVER-WHITE — more gray than the other three (Fe pigmentation), the only non-silvery member of the quartet. Strong anisotropism. Solid solution with safflorite (Radcliffe & Berry 1968 Am. Min. 53:1856) but structural rather than complete; natural Co-Fe arsenides show a miscibility gap around (Co₀.₅Fe₀.₅)As₂. WIDEST temperature range of the quartet (150-450°C) — Fe is rarely limiting, so löllingite forms across the full arsenide-stage T window. In five-element veins specifically, forms the OUTERMOST RIMS at 200-280°C as fluid Fe activity rises after Co and Ni depletion (Markl X_Fe → 1.0 at youngest rims).
