CRITICAL phase boundary with arsenopyrite (FeAsS): at fS₂ > ~10⁻¹² atm (T ~300°C), the system flips to arsenopyrite instead of löllingite (Kretschmar & Scott 1976 Can. Min. 14:364; Heinrich & Eadington 1986). The cleanest binary switch in the four-mineral system — modeled explicitly here as the S < 1 ppm gate. Löllingite + arsenopyrite oscillatory intergrowths are pathognomonic of fluctuating fS₂. Field discriminator: STEEL-GRAY color (the only non-silvery diarsenide); tarnishes dull gray (not iridescent like skutterudite). Striated prisms — striations DEEPER and more regular than arsenopyrite's, a hand-lens-grade distinction. Supergene → SCORODITE FeAsO₄·2H₂O (pale-green to bluish — distinct from cobalt/nickel blooms). NO erythrite/annabergite from pure löllingite — the supergene fingerprint that separates Fe-end from Co/Ni-end arsenides at outcrop. Refs: research dossier 2026-05; Radcliffe & Berry 1968; Pearson 1965 Zeits. Krist. 121:449-462; Kretschmar & Scott 1976 (the fS₂ boundary); Handbook of Mineralogy; Markl et al. 2016.

Fe₃O₄ — mixed-valence Fe²⁺Fe³⁺₂O₄ spinel oxide. Black, metallic-to-submetallic, strongly magnetic (lodestone is natural permanent-magnet magnetite). Forms at the hematite-magnetite (HM) redox buffer — one of geochemistry's most important reference frames. Crossing the HM boundary transforms the entire mineral assemblage. Octahedral {111} and rhombic dodecahedral {110} are the classic habits; martite pseudomorph is magnetite after oxidation to hematite at the crystal surface. Streak: black (diagnostic against hematite's red streak).

Cu₂(CO₃)(OH)₂, the green copper carbonate. Low-T supergene — forms where chalcopyrite oxidizes in CO₂-rich groundwater. Banded botryoidal masses have been prized for decoration since the Bronze Age, from Egyptian amulets to Russian palace columns.

FeS₂, the orthorhombic dimorph of pyrite — same formula, different crystal structure. Acidic (pH<5), low-T (<240°C) fluids switch FeS₂ from cubic pyrite to orthorhombic marcasite. Diagnostic cockscomb and spearhead habits, paler brass than pyrite with iridescent tarnish. Metastable: converts to pyrite over geologic time or on heating, and rots in humid air to sulfuric acid and iron sulfate (the classic museum-specimen problem).

Na₂Ca₂Al₆Si₉O₃₀·8H₂O — orthorhombic (Fdd2) framework silicate, the ORDERED Na-Ca intermediate of the fibrous natrolite group. Its giant b-axis (~56.6 Å) is the structural signature: an ordered stack of one natrolite-type (Na) layer to two scolecite-type (Ca) layers along b, giving the ideal Na₂Ca₂ per 30-O formula — this is why mesolite needs BOTH Na and Ca present, unlike Ca-only scolecite or Na-only natrolite. H 5, density 2.26, vitreous/silky, white to colorless; pyroelectric. The diagnostic habit is the finest hair-like / cottony fibrous tufts (finer than scolecite). Low-Si (Si/Al≈1.5), forms with scolecite earlier than the sheet zeolites; first described from the Cyclopean Islands, Sicily (1816), superb at Poona/Pashan Hills (Deccan) and Nova Scotia. Field discriminator: orthorhombic → PARALLEL extinction (vs scolecite's oblique), finer fiber than both scolecite and natrolite, biaxial (+). Refs: Anthony et al. Handbook of Mineralogy (mesolite); Artioli, Smith & Pluth 1986 Acta Cryst. C42:937 (Fdd2, giant b, layer-ordering); Alberti, Pongiluppi & Vezzalini 1982 N.Jb.Min.Abh. 143:231.

Ca(UO₂)₂(PO₄)₂·8H₂O — autunite with three water molecules gone. Tetragonal uranyl phosphate; appears in the simulator only as a paramorph product of autunite, after heat (>80°C) or sustained dry-air exposure drives the irreversible dehydration. External crystal shape is preserved (the square tabular {001} habit, the lemon-yellow color, the field marks all inherited from the parent autunite); the lattice has lost ~27% of its structural water and partially collapsed. Specific gravity slightly higher (3.45 vs autunite's 3.14); luster duller; fluorescence weaker (still present — uranyl chromophore survives the dehydration, just dampened). MOST AUTUNITE SPECIMENS IN MUSEUMS are actually meta-autunite — fresh autunite has typically been on a shelf for years before reaching a collector. The dehydration is irreversible: once water leaves the structure, it doesn't come back, even in 100% humidity. Sources: research/minerals/research-autunite.md §Variants 1-2 (boss canonical); Roberts, Ansell, Bonardi 1980 — group structural studies. (Bonazzi et al. — autunite-group dehydration thermodynamics.)

HgS (β-HgS) — isometric F-43m SPHALERITE-TYPE structure, the LOW-T cubic polymorph of cinnabar (α-HgS, trigonal P3₁21 helical chains). Hardness 3, density 7.65 g/cm³ (slightly less than cinnabar's 8.10 — cubic close-packing is less efficient than helical chains). IRON-BLACK TO GRAYISH-BLACK with metallic-submetallic luster on fresh surfaces; streak BLACK (diagnostic vs cinnabar's SCARLET streak — the single most striking visual discriminator). Brittle to sectile. Opaque in thin section (cinnabar transmits red; metacinnabar doesn't). Polymorph relations: Potter & Barnes 1978 Econ. Geol. 73:282 established the equilibrium inversion at 344 ± 2°C — above, cinnabar is thermodynamically stable; below, metacinnabar is metastable. BUT metacinnabar nucleates more readily than cinnabar from aqueous sulfide solutions at T < 200°C because the cubic close-packing requires less ordering than cinnabar's helical chains (the kinetic vs thermodynamic divergence). White & Roberson 1962 GSA SP 73 documented metacinnabar at Sulphur Bank precipitating directly at 60-90°C spring waters. Conversion metacinnabar → cinnabar at low T is reconstructive + slow (10³-10⁵ years at 80°C natural residence; effectively quenched at surface T). Required reagents: dissolved Hg²⁺ + reduced S + acidic (pH 1-6.5) + cooling/dilution. Fe/Zn impurities (>5 ppm) stabilize the cubic structure. Type localities Almadén Spain + McDermitt Nevada + Sulphur Bank California. Substrate priority: cinnabar (epitactic, both share Hg-S bonds, the Sulphur Bank surface texture) > opal sinter > native_sulfur. Refs: research dossier 2026-05; White & Roberson 1962; Potter & Barnes 1978; Bailey 1959 USGS Bull. 1148; Dickson & Tunell 1959 Am. J. Sci. 257:341; Anthony et al. Handbook of Mineralogy v.I.

Cu(UO₂)₂(PO₄)₂·8H₂O — torbernite with four water molecules gone. Tetragonal uranyl phosphate; appears in the simulator only as a paramorph product of torbernite, after heat (>75°C) or sustained dry-air exposure drives the irreversible loss of 4 of the 12 structural H₂O. The emerald-green color persists but pales toward apple-green / yellow-green as the lattice collapses; specific gravity rises (3.7 vs torbernite's 3.22); crystals become slightly more friable along the {001} cleavage. Critically: in the Schneeberg / Cornwall museum collections, very few specimens are now fresh torbernite — the trip from a damp mine adit to a dry display case is exactly what triggers the transformation. Like meta-autunite, the conversion is IRREVERSIBLE: even returning a metatorbernite to 100% humidity will not re-hydrate the lattice. Sources: research/minerals/research-torbernite.md §Dehydration Transformation (boss canonical 3bfdf4a).

Cu(UO₂)₂(AsO₄)₂·8H₂O — zeunerite with four water molecules gone. Tetragonal uranyl arsenate; the As-anion analog of metatorbernite (the two are isostructural just as the parents are). Appears in the simulator only as a paramorph product of zeunerite, after heat (>75°C) or dry-air exposure drives the irreversible 12→8 H₂O collapse. Color paler than zeunerite's emerald green, trending grass-green or yellow-green; specific gravity rises (3.85 vs zeunerite's ~3.4). Same museum-storage problem as zeunerite — most cabinet specimens labeled 'zeunerite' from Schneeberg, Cornwall, or Wittichen are actually metazeunerite, dehydrated decades ago. Cu²⁺ still quenches the uranyl emission, so non-fluorescent. The Schneeberg cation+anion fork mechanic still applies at nucleation time; only the dehydration follows. Sources: research/minerals/research-zeunerite.md §Dehydration Transformation; Pinch & Wilson 1977.

NiS — trigonal nickel sulfide, brass-yellow to bronze-yellow metallic. Mohs 3-3.5, the rare nickel mineral that grows as hair-thin acicular needles in geode cavities. Forms in lower-T regimes than nickeline (NiAs); when As is depleted and Ni + S remain, NiS takes the field. The capillary habit is so distinctive that 'millerite' is shorthand among collectors for any radiating-needle sulfide. Showcase localities: Halls Gap (Kentucky), Sterling Hill (NJ), Glamorgan (Wales). Sources: research/minerals/research-millerite.md (boss commit f2939da), Bayliss 1969 (Geochim. Cosmochim. Acta 33).

Pb₅(AsO₄)₃Cl — the 'mimic,' so named because it's isostructural with pyromorphite and distinguishable only by chemistry. Hexagonal prisms and the famous campylite barrels (Cumbria). Supergene product of galena oxidation in As-bearing groundwater.

Na₂SO₄·10H₂O — Glauber salt. The cold-evaporite of the sodium-sulfate system. Stable only below 32.4°C (the eutectic with thenardite); warm above that and the lattice loses 10 water molecules and inverts to thenardite. Forms in winter playas, Antarctic dry valleys, cold caves — anywhere a Na-rich brine cools without freezing. The transparent prismatic crystals are stable enough to handle in cold weather but lose their water in warm dry rooms. Most museum specimens are tincal-style: the mirabilite went away decades ago and the white powdery thing in the case is thenardite pseudomorph.

MoS₂, the primary molybdenum ore. Soft hexagonal platy crystals (Mohs 1-1.5), bluish-gray, greasy — looks like graphite but with a greenish streak. In porphyry systems Mo arrives in a SEPARATE pulse from Cu (Bingham Canyon, Seo et al. 2012), a late magmatic fluid delivering molybdenum on its own timeline.

Be₃Al₂Si₆O₁₈ with Mn²⁺ — the pink-to-peach variety of beryl. Mn²⁺ sits in the Al octahedral site; natural irradiation over geologic time partially oxidizes it to Mn³⁺, producing the pink hue. Named by George F. Kunz of Tiffany & Co (1911) for J.P. Morgan. Late-stage pegmatite mineral — Mn accumulates in fluid while earlier phases (feldspar, quartz, aquamarine) crystallize. Pala District CA, Madagascar, Minas Gerais are top sources.

Pb(Cu,Zn)VO₄(OH) — orthorhombic Pb-Cu vanadate, the Cu end of the descloizite-mottramite series. Olive-green to yellowish-green from the Cu chromophore (distinguishing it at a glance from cherry-red descloizite), Mohs 3-3.5. Type locality: Mottram St. Andrew, Cheshire (England), 1876. Tsumeb produces the museum-grade specimens. Cu/Zn ratio dispatch: when Zn ≥ Cu, descloizite takes priority. Sources: research/minerals/research-mottramite.md (boss commit f2939da).

As — elemental arsenic, the residual-overflow native element. Trigonal (R3̄m), Mohs 3-4, perfect basal {0001} cleavage that splits like dark mica. Tin-white to steel-gray metallic on fresh fracture, tarnishes to arsenolite (As₂O₃) within hours. Forms only when every other As-consumer in the fluid (Fe → arsenopyrite, Ni → nickeline, Co → safflorite, S → realgar/orpiment) has had its share — the leftover phase. Famous Co-Ni-Ag vein districts (Freiberg Saxony, Sainte-Marie-aux-Mines Alsace, Příbram Czech) host native arsenic as the residual after the Co/Ni/Ag captured the metals and S was already locked in. Sources: research/minerals/research-native-arsenic.md (boss commit f2939da), Schiferl 1969 (Acta Cryst. B25), Petruk 1971 (Cobalt-Ag paragenesis).

Bi — elemental native bismuth. Silver-white on fresh surface, iridescent oxide tarnish (yellow, blue, pink) develops rapidly. Melts at an unusually low 271.5°C — the lowest of any native metal. Forms only when sulfur runs out before bismuth does — bismuthinite uses the available S first, then residual Bi crystallizes native. The rainbow 'hoppered' Bi crystals sold in rock shops are lab-grown, not natural; natural native bismuth is typically arborescent/massive/rarely rhombohedral.

Cu — elemental native copper. Only forms when S²⁻ is absent (otherwise precipitates as sulfide) AND Eh is strongly reducing (otherwise oxidizes to cuprite/malachite). The Michigan Keweenaw peninsula basalt vesicles produced 500-ton masses from basalt-hosted brines. Copper-red fresh, tarnishes brown, eventually green (malachite coating). The Statue of Liberty's iconic patina IS malachite growing on native copper — the reverse of supergene ore formation, where rain and air turn metal into mineral in front of us.

Au — elemental native gold, the noble metal. Two precipitation pathways the sim collapses into one supersaturation function: (1) high-T magmatic-hydrothermal Au-Cl complex destabilization at boiling/decompression (Bingham vapor-plume mechanism per Landtwing et al. 2010), and (2) low-T supergene Au-Cl reduction at the redox interface, often coupled with chalcocite enrichment (Bisbee oxidation-cap mechanism per Graeme et al. 2019). Tolerates both oxidizing AND reducing fluids because the two transport complexes (Au-Cl and Au-HS) cover both Eh regimes. Crystal habits range from octahedral {111} (slow growth, rare) through dendritic / spongy (the diagnostic supergene Au) to massive nuggets (rapid precipitation in pockets). Color goes from rich yellow at pure Au through pale yellow electrum (>10% Ag alloy) to rose-gold cuproauride affinity (Cu-rich systems like Bisbee). Essentially indestructible in surface conditions — no acid-dissolution path in the engine.

Ag — elemental silver, the only native element bright enough to make you rich just by looking at it wrong. Cubic isometric (Fm3̄m), Mohs 2.5-3, specific gravity 10.5 (one of the heaviest native metals). The S-depletion mineral: native silver only forms where every sulfur atom is already claimed and the fluid is strongly reducing — the inverse of normal supersaturation logic. Famous wire-silver localities (Kongsberg Norway, Keweenaw Michigan, Cobalt Ontario) all sit in S-depleted reducing pockets. Tarnishes inevitably to a dark acanthite rind from atmospheric H₂S; freshly broken surfaces still flash with the brightest metallic luster known to mineralogy. Source: research/minerals/research-native-silver.md (boss commit f2939da), Boyle 1968 (GSA Bulletin 79), Bjørlykke 1959 (NGU 207).

S — elemental sulfur, the bright canary-yellow native non-metal built from crown-shaped S₈ rings. Orthorhombic α-S (room T) or monoclinic β-S (T>95.5°C, unstable below). Mohs 1.5-2.5, fragile, thermally sensitive — a warm hand can crack a cool specimen. The synproportionation mineral: native S lives on the H₂S/SO₄²⁻ redox boundary where the reaction H₂S + SO₄²⁻ → 2S⁰ + H₂O drops elemental S out of solution. Forms in volcanic fumaroles (Vulcano, El Desierto), salt-dome caprocks via Desulfovibrio bacterial sulfate reduction (Tarnobrzeg), and Sicilian sulfur-vug evaporites with celestine companions (Agrigento — type locality, crystals to 20+ cm). Sources: research/minerals/research-native-sulfur.md (boss commit f2939da), Holland 1965 (Econ. Geol. 60).

Te — elemental tellurium, the rarest of the residual-overflow native trio. Trigonal (P3₁21), Mohs 2-2.5, SG 6.2, perfect {1010} prismatic cleavage. Tin-white to steel-gray metallic, tarnishes to TeO₂ within days of exposure. Tellurium is rarer than platinum in Earth's crust; native Te only crystallizes when every telluride-forming metal (Au → calaverite/sylvanite, Ag → hessite, Pb → altaite, Bi → tetradymite, Hg → coloradoite) has had its fill — a relic of excess. Type localities: Cripple Creek (Colorado), Kalgoorlie (Western Australia, the richest Au-Te deposit on Earth), Emperor Mine (Vatukoula, Fiji). Sources: research/minerals/research-native-tellurium.md (boss commit f2939da), Spry & Thieben 1996 (Mineralium Deposita 31).

Ag2Se — the silver-selenide end-member, sister to hessite (Ag2Te). Forms in selenium-enriched epithermal veins where S is suppressed; wins over acanthite (Ag2S) when Se ≫ S, which is rare globally. Phase transition at 133°C (orthorhombic ↔ cubic) — the high-T cubic form has unusual ionic conductivity (2 S/cm). Type region: Harz Mountains (Germany), where the selenide-bearing low-S hydrothermal veins were first characterized in the 19th century. De Lamar Mine (Idaho) is the major US producer of selenide-type silver ore. Forms a continuous Te ↔ Se substitution series with hessite.

NiAs — hexagonal nickel arsenide, the namesake of the NiAs structure-type. Pale copper-red metallic on fresh fracture, the diagnostic color that fooled early miners into mistaking it for copper ore (the 'kupfernickel' = copper-devil etymology). Mohs 5-5.5, SG 7.8. Forms in high-T reducing veins where Ni and As are present together; cooler / As-poor regimes push the chemistry to millerite (NiS) or annabergite (the supergene Ni arsenate). Type-locality habit at Cobalt, Ontario; also documented at Schneeberg (Saxony), Příbram (Czech), and Tunaberg (Sweden). Sources: research/minerals/research-nickeline.md (boss commit f2939da), Petruk 1971.

Cu₂AsO₄(OH) — orthorhombic Cu arsenate, the Cu end of the olivenite-adamite series. Olive-green to grayish-green (the Cu chromophore — olive in name and color), Mohs 3-4. Forms in Cu-rich supergene oxidation zones; Cornwall is the type locality, with Tsumeb and Bisbee producing showcase modern specimens. Cu/Zn ratio dispatch: when Zn > Cu, adamite (the Zn-end-member of the same arsenate structure) takes priority. Sources: research/minerals/research-olivenite.md (boss commit f2939da).

SiO₂·nH₂O — AMORPHOUS-to-short-range-ordered SILICA MINERALOID (no fixed composition; n typically 3-21 wt% H₂O, most commonly 6-10%). Hardness 5.5-6.5 (lower than quartz at 7 — diagnostic), density 1.9-2.3 g/cm³ (varies with hydration), refractive index 1.40-1.46. Color: white/gray/yellow/brown/red/green/blue depending on impurities (Fe → red-brown, organics → black, Cr/Ni → green); 'precious opal' shows play-of-color from regular ~150-400 nm SiO₂ sphere packing (Sanders 1964 Nature 204:1151); 'common opal' lacks this ordering. THREE STRUCTURAL VARIETIES (Jones & Segnit 1971 J. Geol. Soc. Aust. 18:57; Langer & Flörke 1974 Fortschr. Mineral. 52:17): opal-A (amorphous, broad hump near 4 Å, no Bragg peaks); opal-CT (disordered cristobalite-tridymite stacking); opal-C (sharper cristobalite peaks). Brittle CONCHOIDAL fracture (textbook reference example). NO cleavage. Forms at T < 100°C from silica-supersaturated waters (>200-300 ppm SiO₂ at 25°C per Fournier 1977 Geothermics 5:41), pH 7-9 optimal alkaline silica regime. DIAGENESIS LADDER: opal-A → opal-CT → opal-C → chalcedony → quartz; each step releases structural water + requires aging time / temperature. Engine tracks crystal._diagenesis_stage flag based on T + crystal_zones.length. Hot-spring sinter is the canonical habit — Yellowstone (geyserite), Steamboat Springs Nevada, Sulphur Bank California, Wairakei NZ all build sinter aprons from opal-A. Botryoidal + reniform + nodular + stalactitic forms. SPECTACULAR replacement habits: opalized wood (cell-by-cell), opalized bone, opalized shells. The 'universal binder' of hot-spring deposits — nucleates on rocks, plants, microbial mats (thermophilic cyanobacteria templating spheroidal opal at Yellowstone, well-documented), prior opal layers, sulfide grains. Field discriminator: H 5.5-6.5 (lower than quartz 7), conchoidal fracture without crystal faces, lower density + RI than quartz. Refs: research dossier 2026-05; Jones & Segnit 1971; Langer & Flörke 1974; White & Roberson 1962 GSA SP 73 (Sulphur Bank sinter); Fournier 1977 Geothermics 5:41 (silica solubility); Sanders 1964; Williams & Crerar 1985 J. Sediment. Petrol. 55:312 (diagenesis kinetics); Anthony et al. Handbook of Mineralogy v.II.

As₂S₃ — monoclinic arsenic sulfide (the higher-S phase of the As–S system). Brilliant golden-yellow to lemon-yellow, pearly luster on cleavage. Soft (1.5-2 hardness), perfect {010} cleavage producing the characteristic foliated 'gilded plates'. Low-T hot-spring + epithermal habit; co-occurs with realgar (AsS) in the same fluid systems. The 'aurum pigmentum' of antiquity (the source of the name; ancient/medieval alchemists believed it contained gold). Type locality Allchar, North Macedonia. Major producers Getchell + Twin Creeks (Nevada Carlin-type deposits), Shimen (China), Hunan. Photo-stable (unlike realgar).

As4S4 — monoclinic arsenic sulfide. STRUCTURAL ISOMER of realgar (same As4S4 composition, different As-cage symmetry: realgar D2d, pararealgar Cs). Bright yellow (vs realgar's orange-red), softer (Mohs 1-1.5 vs 1.5-2). Forms EXCLUSIVELY as a light-induced transformation product of realgar over weeks to years of visible-light (>500 nm) exposure. The transformation is IRREVERSIBLE — once realgar becomes pararealgar, it doesn't go back. The yellow powder that crumbles out of old realgar specimens in museum drawers IS pararealgar. The only light-induced transformation modeled in the simulator. Storage in the dark preserves realgar indefinitely; exposure to ordinary room light slowly destroys it. (Bonazzi et al. 1996 Mineralogical Magazine; Roberts et al. 1980.)

NaCa₂Si₃O₈(OH) — triclinic Na-Ca single-chain inosilicate. H 4.5-5, density 2.84-2.90, silky to vitreous luster, perfect {100} + {001} cleavage, conchoidal fracture. The CABBAGE-PETAL / RADIATING-SPRAY habit is the species signature — acicular crystals fanning from a common center. Three settings: (1) Rodingite metasomatism (Jeffrey Mine Quebec — Bernardini 1981 MR 12(5):277 documents the iconic spray-on-grossular habit; Italian Alps; Outokumpu FI; New Idria CA), (2) Late-stage basalt-amygdale fillings (Bay of Fundy NS; New Jersey diabase; Iceland; with native copper at Lake Superior), (3) LARIMAR (Cu-bearing blue gem variety) — Filipos & Frantz 1979 Bahoruco Range Dominican Republic; the Cu²⁺-O charge transfer at trace levels gives the diagnostic sky-blue. Larimar fires through this same engine but with Cu > 0.5 ppm dispatch. Discriminator from analogous fibrous Ca-silicates: wollastonite has no Na, no OH; pectolite has both. Refs: Anthony JW et al. Handbook of Mineralogy v.IIB Single-Chain Silicates; Deer WA, Howie RA, Zussman J Rock-Forming Minerals v.2A; Filipos PJ & Frantz JD (1979) Larimar — A blue pectolite from Hispaniola. Geological Magazine 116:323; Bernardini GP (1981) MR 12(5):277.

CaHAsO₄·2H₂O — monoclinic hydrated calcium hydrogen arsenate. Forms colorless to white delicate radiating/stellate aggregates resembling starbursts of needles — the diagnostic field marker. Vitreous to pearly luster, soft (Mohs 2-2.5). The classic supergene bloom of the Jáchymov (Joachimsthal, Czech) + Schneeberg + Cobalt-Ontario silver-cobalt-arsenic mining districts, where the weathering of cobaltite/nickeline/arsenopyrite primaries releases As⁵⁺ into Ca-rich groundwater. Trace Fe gives yellowish tint, Mn pinkish, Cu greenish — useful provenance fingerprints. Efflorescent: loses water in dry air, converting to haidingerite (CaHAsO₄·H₂O) at ~80-100°C and to anhydrous Ca arsenate at ~150°C, both effectively irreversible. Most field specimens are already partially dehydrated by the time they reach a collection. Highly soluble in dilute HCl/HNO₃; releases toxic arsenic + calcium on dissolution. Type locality: Riegelsdorf, Hesse, Germany (Stromeyer 1819) — but the Jáchymov + Schneeberg displays are the iconic specimens. Sources: research/arcs/research-cation-sinks-orphan-solutes-2026-08-08.md; Anthony et al. Handbook of Mineralogy Vol. IV; Stromeyer 1819 (type-locality description).

PbAl₃(PO₄)₂(OH)₅·H₂O — trigonal Pb-Al-PO₄ supergene endmember, alunite supergroup (beudantite group). At Roughton Gill it forms late in the Pb-PO₄ supergene sequence, after pyromorphite, as cobalt-blue to lavender botryoidal crusts encrusting locally arsenian pyromorphite; surviving green parent tips may remain visible. The simulator therefore models a coexisting encrusting overgrowth and does not claim mass-balanced pseudomorphic replacement. Type locality Roughten Gill (Caldbeck Fells, Cumbria, England) — Hartley J. (1882) MinMag 5:21 original description; Förtsch E.B. (1967) MinMag 36:530 re-examined the type material by X-ray + IR + optical methods and showed it to be a plumbogummite-hinsdalite-hidalgoite mix-crystal (alunite-supergroup endmember nomenclature; a 7.018 Å, c 16.784 Å trigonal; ω 1.680, ε 1.698). The Cu trace at typical supergene levels (1-15 ppm) drives the diagnostic blue color; pure Pb-Al-PO₄ would be lavender-to-white. Found at many other UK supergene localities (Force Crag, Saddleback Old Mine, Sweet Home Mine analogs) but Roughten Gill remains the type and the most-cited specimen source. References: Hartley J. (1882) MinMag 5:21 type description; Förtsch E.B. (1967) MinMag 36:530 type-material correction; Russell A. (1925) MinMag 20:257 revisit; Bridges et al. (2011) JRS 14:3 modern Roughten Gill review; Cooper M.P. & Stanley C.J. (1990) Minerals of the English Lake District: Caldbeck Fells (canonical monograph).

CaMoO4 — the supergene oxidation product of molybdenite. Forms when MoS2 weathers in the oxidation zone: S²⁻ is lost as sulfate, Mo⁶⁺ pairs with available Ca²⁺ from host carbonate, and powellite crystallizes as thin tabular plates with adamantine luster. Same crystal structure as scheelite (CaWO4); powellite-scheelite forms a continuous solid-solution series, and intermediate compositions (yellow with blue/black W-rich zones) are common. Diagnostic UV fluorescence: bright yellow under SW (vs. scheelite's blue) — the difference is W vs. Mo activator in the same lattice. Nasik (India) Deccan basalt cavities are the modern aesthetic reference; Bingham Canyon (Utah) is the canonical porphyry-Cu-Mo oxidation occurrence.

Ca₂Al₂Si₃O₁₀(OH)₂ — orthorhombic Ca-Al phyllosilicate (sheet silicate). H 6-6.5, density 2.80-2.95, vitreous luster, pale-green characteristic color from Fe³⁺ trace. The CLASSIC pale-green botryoidal habit is one of the most-recognized cabinet aesthetics — Lake Superior basalt amygdales (Keweenaw + Isle Royale; Bornhorst 2017 GSA Memoir 213), Iceland amygdales, Alpine fissures (Switzerland Tauern + French Alps), Italian Val di Fassa, rodingite at Jeffrey Mine Quebec + Outokumpu Finland. Important substrate for: datolite + epidote + zeolite-group minerals (heulandite + stilbite + analcime). Discriminator from analogous Ca-Al silicates: zoisite/epidote have +Fe in the Y site; vesuvianite has +Mg; lawsonite is the higher-P endmember (subduction); grossular is the orthosilicate garnet. The pale-green color is dominantly from Fe³⁺ trace (5-50 ppm) — pure Ca-Al prehnite is white-colorless but is rare in collected specimens. Refs: Anthony Handbook v.IIA Phyllosilicates; Deer Howie Zussman v.1B; Liou JG (1971) Synthesis and stability relations of prehnite, Ca2Al2Si3O10(OH)2. American Mineralogist 56:507-531 (definitive stability + zeolite-facies parageneses); Bornhorst TJ 2017 GSA Memoir 213.

Ag₃AsS₃ — the 'LIGHT RUBY SILVER' (Lichtrotgültigerz), trigonal R3c sulfosalt, scarlet-vermilion to cochineal red. Hardness 2-2.5, density 5.57-5.64 g/cm³, distinct {1011} rhombohedral cleavage, brittle-to-sectile, adamantine luster. STREAK BRICK-RED to vermilion — the field discriminator from pyrargyrite (purplish-red). PHOTODECOMPOSES — within hours to days of bright light, surface darkens to black via formation of acanthite + arsenic-bearing residue. Irreversible. Curatorial standard: dark storage. Forms late in epithermal Ag systems at 150-300°C, post-arsenide + post-main-sulfide stage, syn-to-post-native silver. Type localities Jáchymov + Chañarcillo (Chile, world-class crystals). Discriminates from pyrargyrite via the As:Sb FORK MECHANISM in fluid: X_As = mol(As)/(mol(As)+mol(Sb)). X_As > 0.5 → proustite; sweet spot X_As > 0.7 (pure As-end). Below the solvus (~200°C) the system fractionates: proustite first (As more stable per mol), then pyrargyrite from Sb-enriched residue — meaning proustite tends to be EARLIER in zoned veins. Trigonal R3c isostructural with pyrargyrite; complete solid solution above ~300°C, discrete grains below. Supergene: oxidation releases 50% native_Ag + 50% acanthite by mol + AsO₄³⁻ (→ scorodite if Fe present, else arsenolite). Refs: research dossier 2026-05; Sack & Loucks 1985 Am. Min. 70:1270-1289 (canonical Cu-As-Sb-S sulfosalt thermodynamics); Ondruš et al. 2003 J. Geosci. 48:157-192 (Jáchymov paragenesis); Keighin & Honea 1969 (proustite-pyrargyrite phase diagram); Dana 7th vol. I; Handbook of Mineralogy.

Ag₃SbS₃ — the 'DARK RUBY SILVER' (Dunkelrotgültigerz), trigonal R3c sulfosalt, deep cherry-red to red-black (often appears opaque-black until fresh-fractured). Hardness 2.5, density 5.82-5.86 g/cm³ (denser than proustite — Sb is heavier than As). STREAK PURPLISH-RED — the field discriminator from proustite (brick-red/scarlet). Photodecomposes (Ag₂S surface, slower than proustite — weeks to months under light). The MORE COMMON of the two ruby silvers (Sb is more abundant than As in most epithermal Ag systems); roughly an order of magnitude more abundant in collections. Forms late in epithermal Ag systems at 100-300°C, syn-to-post-proustite (Sb fractionation residue — proustite drains As first, then pyrargyrite from residual Sb). Type locality Andreasberg (Harz, Germany); spectacular crystals from San Cristóbal Bolivia, Guanajuato Mexico, Pribram Czechia, Schneeberg Saxony, Comstock Lode NV. Discriminates from proustite via the As:Sb fork: X_As < 0.5 in fluid; sweet spot X_As < 0.3 (pure Sb-end). Has a rare monoclinic dimorph: pyrostilpnite (low-T Ag₃SbS₃) — analogous to xanthoconite (proustite's dimorph); rare in nature, engine defaults to the trigonal phase. Supergene: oxidation releases 50% native_Ag + 50% acanthite by mol + Sb oxides (cervantite Sb³⁺Sb⁵⁺O₄, stibiconite Sb₂O₆(OH), valentinite/senarmontite Sb₂O₃). Refs: research dossier 2026-05; Sack & Loucks 1985; Ondruš et al. 2003 (Jáchymov); Keighin & Honea 1969 (phase diagram); Dana 7th vol. I; Handbook of Mineralogy.

FeS₂, fool's gold. Enormous T range (25-700°C), always reducing. Oxidation produces goethite/limonite plus sulfuric acid — the acid-mine-drainage reaction. Three common habits: cubic with striated faces, 12-face pyritohedral, and raspberry-shaped framboidal aggregates from sedimentary microbial sulfate reduction.

MnO₂ — tetragonal rutile-structure Mn(IV) oxide (P4₂/mnm, a=4.39 Å, c=2.87 Å), retained as the crystalline high-Eh endmember of the simulator's Mn-oxide family. Iron-black to dark steel-gray with a black streak; well-crystallized material is hard and metallic, while earthy aggregates can be soft and sooty. It can form during strongly oxidizing weathering and in low-temperature hydrothermal veins, including prismatic or radiating polianite-style material after manganite. It is not a morphology label for every black coating. Potter and Rossman (1979) found surface dendrites to be romanechite or hollandite-group material, underground mine dendrites to be todorokite, and many stream/cave coatings to be birnessite; they identified no pyrolusite dendrite. SIM 249 therefore routes low-temperature hydrous films, Ba-rich surface dendrites and Mg-templated mine coatings to first-class birnessite, romanechite and todorokite engines. Pyrolusite has no dendritic habit and competes as a later crystalline endpoint. Sources: Anthony et al. Handbook v.III; Potter & Rossman 1979; Champness 1971; Hem 1963; Post 1999; Birkner & Navrotsky 2017.

Pb₅(PO₄)₃Cl — hexagonal apatite-group phosphate. Barrel-shaped prisms in olive-green, yellow-green, brown, or orange. Forms in supergene oxidation zones when phosphate-bearing meteoric water meets existing Pb minerals — galena, anglesite, cerussite can all be pseudomorphed. Apatite-group solid-solution end-member: pyromorphite–mimetite–vanadinite is one of mineralogy's most complete compositional series. Low toxicity (stable Pb) — pyromorphite is used in environmental remediation of Pb-contaminated soils by feeding the soil phosphate.

The least-soluble generic silica phase in the simulator's Ostwald sequence. Once a fluid has fallen below opal and chalcedony saturation but remains supersaturated with respect to quartz, it grows euhedral trigonal crystals — clear, smoky when Al-bearing and irradiated, or amethyst when Fe-bearing and irradiated. Cryptocrystalline chalcedony and amorphous opal are separate solids with separate growth records.

NiAs₂ — orthorhombic Pnnm (löllingite group), marcasite-type structure. Hardness 5.5-6, density 7.09-7.10 g/cm³. Color tin-white WITH A FAINT PINKISH HUE — the only pink-cast member of the diarsenide quartet (Ni-coordination chromophore), diagnostic. TRIMORPHOUS with pararammelsbergite (orthorhombic Pbca, lower-T polymorph) and krutovite (cubic): rammelsbergite is the higher-T form, kinetically persistent down to surface T in nature. Type locality Schneeberg, Saxony. Strong anisotropism in polished section, especially in blues — strongest of the quartet. Demands Ni-rich, Co-depleted fluid; typically forms after early Co has been stripped into skutterudite cores. Tolerates up to ~3 wt% S in solid, but above that flips to gersdorffite (NiAsS sulfarsenide, not in catalog). Sb substitution up to ~1 wt%. Innermost arsenide when Ni dominates the residual fluid post-native-metal nucleation event (Markl et al. 2016). At Schneeberg [type locality] often forms cores with safflorite mantles — the 'Geyer-type' rosette. Field discriminator: PINKISH-WHITE tint distinguishes from safflorite (pure tin-white), löllingite (steel-gray), and skutterudite (silvery → black-tarnishing). Stays silvery longest of the four — Ni component is passive. Supergene → ANNABERGITE Ni₃(AsO₄)₂·8H₂O (apple-green nickel bloom — type locality Annaberg, Saxony). Refs: research dossier 2026-05; Kjekshus, Rakke & Andresen 1974 Acta Chem. Scand. 28:996; Ramdohr 1969 'The Ore Minerals' 839-845; Handbook of Mineralogy; Ondruš et al. 2003.

PbWO₄ — monoclinic lead tungstate, RARE. Same composition as stolzite but a different crystal system; stolzite (tetragonal) is favored ~90% of the time when both can form (kinetic-preference dispatcher in check_nucleation reflects natural rarity). Honey-yellow to brownish-yellow tabular crystals, Mohs 2.5-3, perfect {100} cleavage. Type locality: Broken Hill, NSW, Australia. Sources: research/minerals/research-raspite.md (boss commit f2939da).

AsS — monoclinic arsenic sulfide (α-realgar; the lower-S phase of the As–S system). Orange-red to vermillion red, brilliant resinous luster, soft (1.5-2 hardness). Low-T hot-spring + epithermal-vein habit; co-occurs with orpiment (As₂S₃) in the same fluids. Type locality Allchar, North Macedonia (also a thallium-anomaly site). World-largest producer is Shimen / Hunan, China. Active hot-spring depositional sites include Yellowstone Norris Geyser Basin + Carbazo Springs. Photo-degrades slowly to pararealgar (yellow) under UV — a known museum-curation problem.

MnCO₃ — the rosy manganese carbonate, the pink mineral of cabinet specimens. Same R3̄c calcite-group structure with Mn²⁺ replacing Ca²⁺. Forms a continuous solid solution toward calcite via the kutnohorite (CaMn carbonate) intermediate, producing the diagnostic agate-like banding when Mn/Ca ratios oscillate. Color is intrinsic (Mn²⁺ chromophore), not a trace activator. Stability requires moderate-to-reducing conditions: aggressive oxidation flips Mn²⁺ to Mn³⁺/Mn⁴⁺ and the surface converts to black manganese oxides (pyrolusite, psilomelane). Forms in epithermal Mn-bearing veins (Capillitas Argentina, Sweet Home Colorado), metamorphosed Mn sediments (N'Chwaning South Africa), and low-T carbonate replacement zones.

Hydrated barium manganese oxide with a 2x3 tunnel framework. The tunnel Ba and water are structural: Ba is a required limiting reagent in the simulator, not a decorative trace. Potter and Rossman (1979) identified surface-exposed manganese dendrites as romanechite or a hollandite-group mineral and found no pyrolusite example. Consequently this phase owns the Ba-rich surface-dendrite field and renders as a wall-parallel branching film or botryoidal crust whose displayed area is derived from its booked mass.

(Cu,Zn)₂(CO₃)(OH)₂ — monoclinic supergene carbonate, the Cu-dominant member of the rosasite-aurichalcite pair. Velvety blue-green botryoidal spheres on weathered Cu-Zn sulfide deposits; the diagnostic habit is sky-blue spherical aggregates on red limonite (Mapimi, Mexico). Forms when chalcopyrite + sphalerite weather together at the supergene front, releasing Cu²⁺ + Zn²⁺ + CO₃²⁻ into shallow groundwater that precipitates the carbonate at near-neutral pH. The Cu:Zn ratio in the parent fluid is the key control: rosasite forms when Cu/(Cu+Zn) > 0.5; aurichalcite forms when the ratio inverts — same broth, different outcome. Mohs 4, blue-green streak, splintery fracture. Type locality: Rosas Mine, Sardinia (1908). Source: Pinch & Wilson 1977 (Tsumeb monograph); research/minerals/research-rosasite.md.

Al₂O₃ + Cr³⁺ — the red chromium-bearing variety of corundum. Cr substitutes for Al at the 100-5000 ppm level in the Al octahedral site; the d-d transitions absorb blue-green and transmit red, plus fluoresce strongly red under UV (the 'ruby laser' physics). Top gem 'pigeon's blood' ruby from Mogok Burma shows medium-dark red with blue undertone from trace Fe + strong Cr fluorescence. Requires SiO₂ undersaturation (shared corundum constraint) AND Cr >= 2 ppm. Below Cr=2 the same corundum crystal would be pink sapphire or colorless.

TiO2, the tetragonal titanium oxide. The canonical 'needle' mineral — slender red-brown to golden prisms with adamantine luster, often as inclusions in quartz (rutilated quartz / Venus hair / Cupid's darts). Forms in alpine-cleft fissures, eclogite-facies metamorphism, and pegmatites whenever titanium concentrates. Diagnostic geniculate (knee) twins on {011} and rare reticulated sixling stars. One of the most chemically resistant minerals known — survives weathering, transport, and burial unchanged.

(Co,Fe)As₂ — orthorhombic Pnnm (löllingite group), marcasite-type structure. Hardness 4.5-5, density 7.20-7.47 g/cm³. Color tin-white, readily tarnishes to dark gray (intermediate reactivity between skutterudite's iridescent-black and löllingite's dull gray). The Co-sink phase of the five-element vein arsenide stage — natural compositions span Co:Fe from ~5:1 (Schneeberg) to ~1:2 (Radcliffe & Berry 1968 Am. Min. 53:1856 solid-solution series with löllingite). Famous for STAR-SHAPED FIVELINGS on {011} (twin law, fivefold pseudo-symmetry). Dimorphous with clinosafflorite (monoclinic). Forms in the rim sequence Ni → Co → Fe as fluid evolves: typically MANTLES rammelsbergite or skutterudite cores at 200-350°C, fO₂ slightly less reducing than skutterudite's regime. Tolerates up to ~0.9 wt% S in the solid before flipping to cobaltite sulfarsenide. Field discriminator: lower hardness than skutterudite/rammelsbergite (4.5-5 vs. 5.5-6); star twins under hand lens pathognomonic when present; tarnishes dull gray (slower than skutterudite's iridescent, faster than rammelsbergite's silver). Practically indistinguishable from rammelsbergite without EMPA — the classic identification problem. Supergene → erythrite crimson bloom. Refs: research dossier 2026-05; Radcliffe & Berry 1968 Am. Min. 53:1856-1881; Handbook of Mineralogy; Kraus & Pollmann 2002 MinRec 33(6) (Schneeberg); Kissin 1992; Markl et al. 2016.

Al₂O₃ with Fe + Ti (blue), Fe alone (yellow), V (violet), or trace Cr (pink-orange padparadscha) — the non-red corundum varieties. Blue sapphire's color is the Fe²⁺-Ti⁴⁺ intervalence charge transfer (IVCT), a well-characterized gem mechanism requiring both cations at the right concentration. Kashmir 'cornflower blue' is the classic; Montana Yogo, Sri Lanka, Madagascar, Thailand/Cambodia are active sources. Shares the SiO₂ < 50 upper gate with corundum + ruby.

CaWO4 — the calcium tungstate, one of the principal W ores and a UV-fluorescence classic. Forms in granitic-intrusion-related W-Sn skarns and in mesothermal vein systems where W concentrates from late-stage granitic fluids and Ca comes from the wallrock. Brilliant blue-white SW UV fluorescence is diagnostic — used since the 19th century to prospect for tungsten in the field. Forms continuous solid-solution series with powellite (CaMoO4); intermediate compositions show duller / yellower fluorescence as Mo replaces W. Panasqueira (Portugal) and Pine Creek (California) are skarn type localities. Recent Chinese tungsten production (Hunan, Jiangxi) dominates global supply.

CaAl₂Si₃O₁₀·3H₂O — monoclinic (Cc, β≈90.64° pseudo-orthorhombic) framework silicate, the Ca-endmember of the fibrous natrolite-group zeolites (natrolite Na → mesolite Na-Ca → scolecite Ca, a coupled Na⁺+½□ ↔ Ca²⁺+½H₂O substitution — the Ca member carries the extra channel water). H 5-5.5, density 2.25-2.29, vitreous/silky, white to colorless; pyroelectric + piezoelectric. The signature habit is radiating acicular sprays and 'puffball' needle bursts, plus slender square-section prisms to 30 cm. Twinning on {100} (twin axis [001]) is near-ubiquitous — it makes the monoclinic crystal mimic tetragonal symmetry. A LOW-silica zeolite (Si/Al≈1.5) that forms EARLIER in the basalt-amygdule paragenesis than the higher-Si sheet zeolites stilbite + heulandite (which drape over the scolecite sprays); the Deccan Traps (Poona/Nashik/Mumbai, Maharashtra) + Teigarhorn, Berufjord, Iceland are the premier localities. Field discriminator: scolecite is the monoclinic member → OBLIQUE (inclined) extinction, vs the parallel extinction of orthorhombic natrolite + mesolite; coarser needles than mesolite. Refs: Anthony et al. Handbook of Mineralogy (scolecite); Alberti, Pongiluppi & Vezzalini 1982 N.Jb.Min.Abh. 143:231 (natrolite-group crystal chemistry); Smith & Walls 1971 Mineral.Mag. 38:72; Ottens et al. 2019 (Deccan).

FeAsO₄·2H₂O, the arsenic-sequestration mineral. Pseudo-octahedral pale blue-green dipyramids; the most common supergene oxidation product of arsenopyrite. Locks AsO₄³⁻ in stable crystals as long as pH stays below 5; above pH 5 it dissolves and releases AsO₄³⁻ for the higher-pH arsenate suite (erythrite, mimetite, adamite, pharmacosiderite). Type locality Freiberg, Saxony; world-class deep-blue crystals at Tsumeb (Gröbner & Becker 1973). Dehydrates to anhydrous FeAsO₄ above 160°C.

CaSO₄·2H₂O, the dihydrate form of gypsum — glassy, water-clear, soft enough to cleave with a fingernail. Stable only below ~60°C, where anhydrite takes over. Naica's cathedral blades grew at a steady 58°C for half a million years, producing the largest natural crystals on Earth.

Cu₅(SiO₃)₄(OH)₂ — deep azure-to-greenish-blue inosilicate (single-chain Cu-silicate; pyroxene-type chains on Cu-O sheets — NOT to be confused with plancheite's amphibole-type double chains; Evans & Mrose 1977 Am. Min. 62:491). Type locality Shattuck mine, Bisbee (Warren district), Arizona (Schaller 1915 J. Wash. Acad. Sci. 5:7). Hardness 3.5, density 4.11 g/cm³ (heavy for a non-metallic silicate due to high Cu content), perfect cleavage on {010} and {100}. Forms strictly supergene at 25-90°C in mildly alkaline (pH 7.5-9.0) oxidizing pore fluids — distinctly more alkaline than dioptase, requiring substantial OH⁻ activity. The defining mechanism is REPLACEMENT OF MALACHITE when CO₂ escapes from a vadose vug: 5 Cu₂(CO₃)(OH)₂ + 8 SiO₂(aq) → 2 Cu₅(SiO₃)₄(OH)₂ + 5 CO₂↑ + 3 H₂O. Higher Cu:Si ratio than dioptase (5:4 vs. 1:1) — shattuckite is the high-Cu, low-Si Cu-silicate. Field discriminator vs. chrysocolla: shattuckite H 3.5 (vs. chrysocolla 2-4 but softer), density 4.1 (vs. chrysocolla 2.0-2.4 — heavy in hand), shows fibrous/acicular radial structure under loupe (chrysocolla is amorphous/conchoidal). Refs: research dossier 2026-05; Schaller 1915 (type description); Evans & Mrose 1977 (structure); Keller 1977 MinRec 8(3) (Tsumeb plancheite-shattuckite-dioptase sequence); Cairncross & Bahmann 2006 MinRec 37:137 (Kaokoveld); Anthony et al. Handbook of Mineralogy v.II.

FeCO₃ — the iron carbonate, a calcite-group mineral (R3̄c) with Fe²⁺ in the Ca site. Tan to deep brown depending on Fe content and trace substitution (manganosiderite ↔ rhodochrosite, ankerite ↔ dolomite). Hard-gated to REDUCING conditions because Fe²⁺ must stay reduced to be soluble; rising O₂ progressively converts siderite to goethite/limonite — the diagenetic 'limonite cube after siderite' pseudomorph mechanism. Forms in MVT veins (accessory), sedimentary ironstone formations, hydrothermal Fe veins, and coal-seam concretions (spherosiderite).

(Co,Ni,Fe)As₃ — cubic Im-3̄ skutterudite-group triarsenide; complete solid solution with nickel-skutterudite (NiAs₃₋ₓ). Hardness 5.5-6, density 6.5-6.82 g/cm³. Color tin-white to silver-gray, tarnishing iridescent then BLACK (the most reactive of the diarsenide quartet — distinctive). Cleavage distinct on {001} and {111}. The defining HIGHEST-temperature member of the five-element vein arsenide stage (Kissin 1992 Geosci. Canada 19:113-124). Triarsenide stoichiometry demands the highest As activity of any phase — X_As = 0.96-0.99 in natural samples (Markl et al. 2016 Min. Dep. 51:703-718, Odenwald compositional study). NO sulfur tolerance — fluid S > 5 ppm pushes the system to cobaltite (CoAsS) instead. Forms FIRST in zoned arsenide rosettes, nucleating directly on native Bi-Ag dendrites at 280-290°C (the Markl 'natural fracking' model: CH₄ or graphite contact rapidly reduces an oxidized As(III)-bearing brine far from equilibrium). Substrate priority: native_bismuth > native_silver > native_arsenic > vug wall. Field discriminator from safflorite/rammelsbergite/loellingite: highest hardness, conchoidal fracture, BLACK iridescent tarnish (the others stay silver/gray longer); in thin section, ISOTROPIC (cubic — the only one of the four). Refs: research dossier 2026-05; Roseboom 1962 Am. Min. 47:310-327; Radcliffe 1971 Can. Min. 9:559-563; Mandel & Donohue 1971 Acta Cryst. 27:2288; Kissin 1992; Markl et al. 2016; Ondruš et al. 2003 J. Geosci. 48:157-192 (Jáchymov three-stage scheme); Anthony et al. Handbook of Mineralogy.

ZnCO₃, zinc's carbonate heir: forms when sphalerite oxidizes in CO₂-bearing groundwater. Named for James Smithson, founder of the Smithsonian. Botryoidal habit is typical; trace Cu gives prized turquoise-blue, Co gives pink, Cd gives yellow.

ZnS, the dominant zinc ore. Classic MVT mineral — forms at 60-200°C where metal brines meet H₂S-bearing groundwater. Iron substitution darkens the color from pale yellow (low-Fe cleiophane) through honey-brown to nearly black marmatite.

LiAlSi₂O₆ — monoclinic pyroxene. Flattened tabular prisms that read as 'book' shape, with two cleavage directions at ~87° producing characteristic parting. Can reach 14 meters — among the longest single crystals on Earth (Etta mine, South Dakota). Lithium accumulates late in pegmatite crystallization because no early mineral takes it, so spodumene is the residual-fluid signature. Kunzite (pink-lilac) from Mn²⁺ substitution shows strong pink-orange SW fluorescence. Hiddenite (green) from Cr³⁺ is rarer. Named for George Kunz, Tiffany's mineralogist, who bought Minas Gerais specimens by the crate.

Sb₂S₃ — orthorhombic antimony sulfide, lead-gray to steel-gray with brilliant metallic luster on fresh cleavage. One of the most visually striking minerals: sword-like elongated blades up to 60 cm at Ichinokawa (Japan). Same structure as bismuthinite (Bi₂S₃) — Sb and Bi are geochemical cousins. Low-melting (550°C), so stibnite is destroyed by minor metamorphism. Primary Sb ore. Dendritic growth when rapidly deposited; single sword-blades when slow.

NaCa₄Si₂₇Al₉O₇₂·28H₂O (stilbite-Ca) — monoclinic (C2/m) framework silicate of the zeolite group. H 3.5-4, density 2.12-2.22, vitreous luster, pearly on {010}; the Deccan endmember is the famous peach-to-salmon colour. The COOLER, more-hydrated member of the stilbite/heulandite dehydration couple: calorimetry (Kiseleva, Navrotsky, Belitsky & Fursenko 2001) gives the reaction Ca-stilbite = Ca-heulandite + H₂O, so stilbite is stable on the cooler/wetter side and dehydrates to heulandite as temperature rises. Signature habit is the wheatsheaf/bowtie sheaf bundle — twinning on {001} is 'extremely common' (Wikipedia/Mindat/IZA), producing the cruciform/hourglass aggregates. Type expression for collectors is the Deccan Traps basalt amygdule (Nashik, Pune, Mumbai, Maharashtra) — the world's premier locality — where peach stilbite perches on a chalcedony/quartz silica veneer with apophyllite, scolecite, mesolite, heulandite and calcite. Field discriminator: stilbite = sheaves/bowties; heulandite = isolated coffin-shaped {010} tablets; stellerite is the orthorhombic (Fmmm) Na-poor analog lacking the bowtie habit; epistilbite rarely forms the large sheaf clusters. Refs: Coombs et al. 1997 Can. Mineral. 35:1571 (nomenclature, stilbite-Ca/-Na); Kiseleva Navrotsky Belitsky & Fursenko 2001 Am. Mineral. 86:448; Anthony et al. Handbook of Mineralogy; Ottens et al. 2019 (Deccan paragenesis); Sukheswala Avasia & Gangopadhyay 1974 Mineral. Mag. (Deccan zonation).

PbWO₄ — tetragonal lead tungstate, the lead analog of scheelite (CaWO₄). Honey-yellow to orange-yellow Mohs 2.5-3, the more common of the two PbWO₄ polymorphs (~90% of natural occurrences vs raspite's monoclinic ~10%). Type locality: Cínovec (Czech Republic). Broken Hill (Australia) and Tsumeb (Namibia) produce the museum specimens — sharp honey-yellow dipyramids. Sources: research/minerals/research-stolzite.md (boss commit f2939da).

SrCO3 — the strontium carbonate, type locality Strontian (Scotland, 1790) and the namesake of the element strontium itself. Aragonite-group orthorhombic carbonate; almost always twinned cyclically into pseudohexagonal forms. Forms in low-T hydrothermal veins where Sr-bearing fluids encounter alkaline carbonate conditions; loses to celestine (SrSO4) when sulfate is the dominant Sr-pairing anion, which is most of the time globally — celestine is far more common because oceans deliver SO4 more freely than CO3. Almost always UV-fluorescent yellow-white and persistently phosphorescent. Münsterland (Germany) acicular sprays and Meckley's Quarry (Pennsylvania) fluorescent specimens are the collectors' references.

(Au,Ag)Te2 with Au:Ag typically 1:1 to 3:1 — the gold-silver telluride that sits between calaverite (pure Au) and hessite (pure Ag) on the telluride spectrum. Photosensitive: prolonged light exposure produces a dark surface tarnish (the gold is still in the lattice but the surface oxidizes). Type locality Sacarîmb / Nagyág (Transylvania, Romania); also Cripple Creek (Colorado), Kalgoorlie (Western Australia), Emperor mine (Vatukoula, Fiji). Miners called it 'graphic tellurium' for the bladed-cuneiform intergrowth pattern. Note: sylvanite ≠ sylvite (KCl) — they share no chemistry, just a Latin root for the same Carpathian forest range.

KCl — the potassium chloride evaporite. Forms in the late stage of evaporite sequences, after halite (NaCl) has already removed most of the sodium and chloride from the brine; sylvite is what crystallizes from the K-enriched residual liquor. More soluble than halite (344 g/L at 25°C vs. halite's 360 g/L is incorrect — sylvite is actually slightly LESS soluble than halite at 25°C, but sylvite's solubility increases sharply with T while halite's barely changes, so cooling brines favor sylvite precipitation late). Deliquescent in humid air. Type locality Stassfurt (Germany, Zechstein evaporites); Carlsbad (New Mexico, Permian basin) and Solikamsk (Russia, Upper Kama) are the major commercial sources. Note: sylvite ≠ sylvanite — different chemistry, similar Latin root.

Cu₁₂As₄S₁₃ — the As-endmember fahlore, paired with tetrahedrite. Same cubic I4̄3m structure; arsenic replaces antimony. Visually indistinguishable from tetrahedrite except by the cherry-red thin-fragment transmission test (tennantite transmits; tetrahedrite stays opaque). On oxidation releases Cu + AsO₄³⁻, feeding the secondary arsenate paragenesis: adamite, erythrite, annabergite, mimetite. Closes the loop between primary copper sulfosalts and downstream supergene arsenates.

Cu₁₂Sb₄S₁₃ — the Sb-endmember 'fahlore,' German miner's term for the steel-gray copper sulfosalts that paid in silver as much as in copper. Hydrothermal 100-400°C, optimum 200-300°C. Cubic I4̄3m space group produces diagnostic {111} tetrahedra. Paired with tennantite (As endmember) in a continuous solid solution: the Sb:As ratio of an ore fluid is recorded directly in the composition. Ag substitutes for Cu to produce the silver ore variety 'freibergite.'

Na₂SO₄ — anhydrous sodium sulfate. The warm-evaporite half of the mirabilite-thenardite pair: where Glauber salt dehydrates above 32°C, thenardite is what’s left, OR what crystallizes directly from warm playa brines that never cool through the eutectic. Orthorhombic dipyramids in well-formed crystals, tabular plates more often, white efflorescent crusts most commonly. Searles Lake CA, Bayan Khar Mongolia, Camp Verde AZ, the type locality at Espartinas Spain.

NaCa₂Al₅Si₅O₂₀·6H₂O — orthorhombic (Pncn, pseudotetragonal) framework silicate, a highly aluminous (Si/Al≈1) basalt-amygdule zeolite. H 5-5.5, density 2.23-2.39, vitreous-pearly; white/yellow/pink/green, often concentrically zoned. The famous 'thomsonite eyes' — radiating spherical botryoidal nodules with concentric colour banding — are the Lake Superior (Isle Royale, Grand Marais MN) gem/lapidary material (the green variety is 'lintonite'). Relative order varies between localities and even neighboring cavities; authored scenarios therefore supply locality-specific paragenetic windows instead of a universal sequence. Being Si/Al≈1, it is favored at LOW silica activity — the clean discriminator from the higher-Si natrolite group (Si/Al≈1.5); the engine uses a soft low-silica preference (Na/Ca does NOT cleanly separate thomsonite from mesolite — both are Na-Ca, thomsonite just more-Ca + lower-Si). Type locality Old Kilpatrick, Dunbartonshire, Scotland (named for Dr Thomas Thomson). Field discriminator: the concentric spherical eyes are diagnostic; biaxial (+); orthorhombic (vs monoclinic scolecite/mesolite); much of Lake Superior 'thomsonite' is actually prehnite/mesolite by XRD — distinguish by hardness + optics. Refs: Anthony et al. Handbook of Mineralogy (thomsonite-Ca); Wise & Tschernich 1978 Can.Mineral. 16:487; Coombs et al. 1997; Gatta et al. 2010 Am.Mineral. 95:495.

nodes.formula: SiO2-rich quartz-crocidolite chatoyant aggregate (origin model disputed)
nodes.redox: model-dependent: reduced/modest-O2 synchronous growth or oxidizing surface overprint
nodes.description: Tiger's-eye is a chatoyant, SiO₂-rich quartz-crocidolite aggregate rather than an IMA mineral species. Its gold-brown optical effect records aligned fibrous fabric plus iron oxidation, but the origin of that fabric is disputed. Heaney & Fisher (2003, Geology 31:323-326) reject pseudomorphic replacement and infer synchronous antitaxial quartz-crocidolite crack-seal growth. Gutzmer, Beukes & Cairncross (2004, Geology 32:e44) use the shallow tiger's-eye → hawk's-eye → crocidolite field transition to argue for later silicification and oxidation of older crocidolite seams; they state the material is not a pseudomorph sensu stricto. The simulator therefore provides both executable interpretations. Tiger iron is the BIF-banded quartz-hematite/jasper aggregate and is a rock/trade variety, not a mineral species.

Na₂B₄O₇·5H₂O — borax with five water molecules gone. The simulator currently represents the common pseudomorph route: the external borax shape is preserved while the lattice dehydrates and the surface blooms white-powdery. Natural Searles Lake also contains primary 1–3 mm tincalconite crystals in contact with brine. The borax–tincalconite reaction is reversible at sufficiently high water activity; rehydration is a declared model boundary until the simulator records humidity and reversible phase history.

CaTiSiO₅ (CaTiO[SiO₄]) — monoclinic (P2₁/a) nesosilicate, the mineral once called sphene. H 5-5.5, density 3.48-3.60, adamantine-to-resinous luster with very high dispersion (the gem 'fire'). The diagnostic habit is the WEDGE-SHAPED (sphenoid) crystal, flattened ∥{001}, commonly a {100} contact or penetration twin; good {110} cleavage, {221} parting from lamellar twinning. Color runs brown / yellow / gray / black / green / red / colorless: brown-to-yellow is the common igneous-metamorphic accessory, while the prized CHROME-GREEN variety (Cr³⁺ → Ti) is the alpine-cleft gem (Tormiq/Alchuri, Pakistan; Tavetsch + St. Gotthard + Zermatt + Göschener Alp, Switzerland). ALPINE-CLEFT titanite is the LOW-T hydrothermal/fissure end of the species — near-end-member Ca-Ti-Si, low-F (Göschener Alp: Ca₁.₀₀(Ti₀.₉₇Fe³⁺₀.₀₃)Si₁.₀₀O₄.₉₆, the Handbook reference analysis), grown LATE on the quartz druse from the cooling cleft fluid (≤~400°C), versus the higher-T (690-740°C magmatic / 250-670°C hydrothermal) disseminated accessory titanite. Common substitutions Al³⁺/Fe³⁺ → Ti⁴⁺ (charge-balanced by F⁻/OH⁻ → O), minor Nb + REE. Discriminator from cousins: adamantine-resinous luster + wedge/sphenoid habit + high dispersion + monoclinic flattening; vs epidote (prismatic, pistachio-green, {001} cleavage); vs olivine/chondrodite (different habit); the brown wedge with 'fire' is unmistakable. Refs: Anthony et al. Handbook of Mineralogy 2001 (titanite sheet — Göschener Alp alpine-cleft analysis); Deer Howie Zussman 1982 Rock-Forming Minerals v.1A pp.443-466; Oberti, Smith, Rossi & Caucia 1991 EJM 3:777-792.

Hydrated manganese oxide with a large 3x3 tunnel framework. Mg-rich interlayers in a birnessite-like precursor template tunnel formation; Golden, Chen and Dixon (1986) produced well-crystallized todorokite by Mg exchange followed by hydrothermal treatment at 155 °C, and Zhao et al. (2015) used reflux treatment to show that interlayer cation identity and Mn oxidation state control conversion. Potter and Rossman (1979) found underground mine dendrites to be todorokite, but did not establish a direct precipitation pathway. The simulator therefore has no bare-wall or room-temperature route: it converts an active, mass-booked birnessite coating in place at 95–200 °C, preserves the precursor Mn inventory, books exchanged Mg at a 1:6 formula ratio, and renders the product as wall-parallel mine dendrites or fibrous mats.

Al₂SiO₄(F,OH)₂ — orthorhombic, prismatic with steep pyramidal terminations and perfect basal cleavage {001}. Imperial topaz from Ouro Preto crystallized at ~360°C, 3.5 kbar from metamorphic hydrothermal fluids (Morteani et al. 2002). Golden-orange to pinkish color from trace Cr³⁺ sourced from nearby ultramafic bodies. Colorless to pale blue when Cr is absent. F/OH ratio in the crystal records fluid composition at growth time. Crystals can snap cleanly along basal cleavage — pocket floors littered with cleavage fragments are diagnostic.

Cu(UO₂)₂(PO₄)₂·12H₂O — tetragonal uranyl phosphate, the P-branch of the autunite-group anion-competition trio (with zeunerite for AsO₄³⁻ and carnotite for VO₄³⁻ the other branches). Forms emerald-green to apple-green thin tabular plates that look like green mica; strongly radioactive (U⁶⁺ in the lattice), notably non-fluorescent (Cu²⁺ quenches uranyl emission). Forms at the supergene oxidation front when uraninite weathers to mobile U⁶⁺ and meets phosphate-bearing groundwater alongside Cu²⁺ — torbernite wins the cation race when P/(P+As) > 0.5 in the local fluid. Mohs 2-2.5, dehydrates irreversibly to metatorbernite (8 H₂O) above ~75°C. Type locality: Schneeberg, Saxony (Ore Mountains). Sources: Pinch & Wilson 1977 monographs; research/minerals/research-torbernite.md (boss commit 3bfdf4a).

Complex cyclosilicate — trigonal, elongated prisms with deep vertical striations and a slightly rounded triangular cross-section. Schorl (black, Fe²⁺-dominant) crystallizes early from pegmatite melt; elbaite (colored, Li-dominant) crystallizes late from residual pocket fluid as Fe depletes and Li accumulates. Striations are growth records — each ridge is a growth pulse. Color is a fluid composition snapshot: Mn²⁺ → pink (rubellite), Cr³⁺/V³⁺ → green (verdelite), Fe²⁺+Ti → blue (indicolite), Cu²⁺ → neon Paraíba blue (extreme rarity). The Jonas mine in Minas Gerais was the world's greatest rubellite producer. The most Minas Gerais mineral there is.

Ca₂Mg₅Si₈O₂₂(OH)₂ — monoclinic Ca-Mg calcic amphibole. H 5-6, density 3.0, vitreous luster, {110} prismatic cleavage at 56°/124°. Forms by metamorphism of impure dolomite (skarn — Manitoba + Lake Baikal + Italian Alps); rodingite-contact assemblages (Jeffrey Mine + Cassiar BC); talc deposits (the documented WHO-recognized health-hazard variety). ASBESTIFORM tremolite is one of six commercial asbestos minerals (the others: chrysotile, actinolite, anthophyllite, amosite, crocidolite). At JEFFREY MINE specifically, tremolite-asbestos is the documented chrysotile contaminant (WHO 1986 IARC Monograph; Frank et al. 2002 — more carcinogenic than chrysotile per epidemiological studies of Jeffrey workers). The mineral identity is geologically + scientifically important regardless of health context. Discriminator from analogous calcic amphiboles: tremolite is the Fe-poor Mg endmember; actinolite is the Fe-bearing intermediate (Fe > ~50 routes to actinolite). Refs: Hawthorne FC et al. (2012) Nomenclature of the amphibole supergroup. American Mineralogist 97:2031; Anthony Handbook v.IIB; Veblen DR & Wylie AG (1993) Mineralogy of amphiboles. Reviews in Mineralogy 28:61; WHO IARC Monograph 100C (2012) Asbestos.

CuAl6(PO4)4(OH)8·4H2O — hydrated copper-aluminum phosphate. The 'sky-blue' supergene mineral, mined since ~5000 BCE (Maghara/Sinai, Nishapur/Iran). Forms in arid Cu-porphyry oxidation zones when meteoric water leaches Cu²⁺ from sulfides and PO₄³⁻ from host apatite. Color from Cu²⁺ chromophore; Fe³⁺ substitution shifts toward green chalcosiderite. Crystallizes essentially only as cryptocrystalline aggregate (botryoidal, veinlet-fill, nodular); discrete triclinic crystals known only from Lynch Station, VA. Distinguishes the supergene Cu zone from chrysocolla (silica), malachite (carbonate), and atacamite (chloride) — the four-axis branching of the Cu oxidation zone keyed to fluid anion chemistry.

Ca(UO₂)₂(VO₄)₂·5-8H₂O — orthorhombic Ca-uranyl vanadate, the cation analog of carnotite. Forms by the same mechanism (oxidizing groundwater + uraninite weathering + V-bearing fluid) but wins when Ca/(K+Ca) > 0.5 — the geological-default cation in sandstone groundwater. The two species are commonly intergrown in Colorado Plateau and Tyuya-Muyun deposits, with Britannica noting they are interconvertible by cation exchange. Canary-yellow earthy crusts staining sandstone, weakly-to-moderately fluorescent yellow-green LW UV (vanadate matrix dampens emission slightly even with Ca-cation; cleaner than carnotite's yellow but not as bright as autunite/uranospinite). Mohs 1.5-2, dehydrates readily to metatyuyamunite (·3-5H₂O) at room T in dry storage. Type locality: Tyuya-Muyun, Fergana Valley, Kyrgyzstan (Nenadkevich 1912). Source: research/minerals/research-tyuyamunite.md (implementation-grade draft, 2026-05-01); cation-fork mechanic mirrors carnotite + the Round 9d torbernite/autunite pair.

UO₂, the primary uranium mineral and gatekeeper for the entire secondary U family. Pitch-black, extremely dense, radioactive. Forms under strongly reducing conditions — any oxygen converts U⁴⁺ to mobile UO₂²⁺ uranyl ion (fed back to broth in v12 oxidation block, feedstock for torbernite/zeunerite/carnotite). Notably non-fluorescent — the ABSENCE of fluorescence distinguishes uraninite from its bright-green secondaries (autunite, torbernite). Each α-decay turns a U atom into Pb; old uraninite accumulates radiogenic lead that eventually precipitates as nearby galena. Source: research/minerals/research-uraninite.md (boss canonical 626bb22, May 2026).

Ca(UO₂)₂(SiO₃)₂(OH)₂·5H₂O — monoclinic P2₁, uranyl-silicate chain structure (uranyl-silicate sheets linked by Ca + 5 H₂O). Hardness 2.5, density 3.83-3.90 g/cm³. Color BRILLIANT lemon to canary yellow; weathered surfaces straw-yellow. Streak pale yellow. Vitreous on fresh crystal faces, silky on fibrous aggregates, dull-earthy on powdery coatings. DIAGNOSTIC BRIGHT YELLOW-GREEN to apple-green FLUORESCENCE under both SW (254 nm) AND LW (365 nm) UV — persistent, not phosphorescent. The fluorescence is from the (UO₂)²⁺ uranyl ion vibronic structure (Burns 2005) and intensity often exceeds autunite's under SW. Forms SUPERGENE strictly at <50°C from oxidative weathering of uraninite/coffinite when Ca²⁺ AND dissolved SiO₂ are both available. pH window 5-8; above 8 carbonate-uranyl species (liebigite, andersonite) dominate; below 5 uranyl-sulfates (johannite, zippeite) win. Requires logfO₂ > –20 (atmospheric). Boltwoodite (K), sklodowskite (Mg), kasolite (Pb) are the cation analogs; uranophane wins when Ca is the available cation. The classic late-supergene uranyl silicate — replaces uraninite/coffinite/pitchblende along fractures + at the oxidation front. Type localities Schneeberg + Jáchymov (alpha form), Marysvale UT, Colorado Plateau. Acicular fibrous habit + bright yellow-green UV fluorescence is the unmistakable field combo. Refs: research dossier 2026-05; Ginderow 1988 Acta Cryst. C44:421 (structure); Finch & Murakami 1999 RIMG 38:91-179 (canonical paragenesis chart fig. 12); Burns 2005 Can. Mineral. 43:1839 (uranyl crystal chemistry); Stohl & Smith 1981 Am. Mineral. 66:610 (uranyl-silicate family); Handbook of Mineralogy 8th ed. v.II; MinRec Schneeberg issue v.19 (1988).

Ca(UO₂)₂(AsO₄)₂·10H₂O — tetragonal Ca-uranyl arsenate, the autunite-group cation analog of zeunerite. Same parent fluid as zeunerite (U + As + supergene-T + oxidizing) but wins when Ca/(Cu+Ca) > 0.5 — typically when Cu has been depleted from the local fluid but As is still around. Strongly fluorescent yellow-green LW UV — Ca²⁺ doesn't quench like Cu²⁺ does in zeunerite, putting uranospinite in the same 'bright fluorescer' tier as autunite (slightly dampened by the heavier As-anion vibrational coupling). Tabular yellow plates that look like a yellow autunite, with the As content as the chemistry giveaway. Mohs 2-3, dehydrates readily to metauranospinite. Type locality: Walpurgis Flacher vein, Weisser Hirsch Mine, Schneeberg, Saxony (Weisbach 1873). Sources: research/minerals/research-uranospinite.md (implementation-grade draft, 2026-05-01); MSA Handbook of Mineralogy.

Pb₅(VO₄)₃Cl — hexagonal apatite-group vanadate. Bright red-orange to brown-orange hexagonal prisms, one of the most recognizable minerals in a collector case. Vanadate end-member of the pyromorphite-mimetite-vanadinite series. Vanadium comes from oxidation of V-bearing sediments (red-bed ironstones, roll-fronts) in arid climates — the ACF mines of Morocco and the Arizona desert have produced the finest specimens. Classified here under phosphate (apatite-group structure); the 12-hue palette has no vanadate class so we fold with P/As/V together.

Ca₁₀(Mg,Fe)₂Al₄(SiO₄)₅(Si₂O₇)₂(OH)₄ — tetragonal P4/nnc Ca-Mg-Al sorosilicate, also widely called IDOCRASE (the older mineralogical name, still used in jewelry trade; vesuvianite was the original Werner 1795 name from Vesuvius type locality). H 6.5, density 3.32-3.43, vitreous luster, tetragonal {100} prismatic habit with square cross-section as default. Forms in three settings, all sharing high-Ca + Mg-or-Al + Si chemistry under alkaline conditions: (1) Rodingite metasomatism — Ca-Al-rich fluid from serpentinization-driven dehydration alters cross-cutting mafic dikes in ultramafic host (Jeffrey Mine Val-des-Sources Quebec — Bernardini GP 1981 MR 12(5):277 is the canonical anchor; Italian Alps Val di Fassa + Val Malenco; New Idria CA; Cassiar BC). Jeffrey's CYPRINE variety — sky-to-deep-blue Cu-bearing vesuvianite — is the cabinet-collector standard for the species; Cu²⁺-O charge transfer at 0.5-5 ppm Cu gives sky-blue, > 5 ppm deepens to azure (Bernardini 1981 figs 12-15; the world reference cyprine material). (2) Contact metamorphism of impure limestone (skarns) — Vesuvius Italy type locality 1795 (the brown-yellow Werner material); Crestmore CA (chromian green); Tellemark Norway; Wessels Mine South Africa (pink manganvesuvianite). (3) Carbonatite-syenite alteration zones — Kovdor Russia + Magnet Cove AR (rare, yellow-brown varieties). Cyprine + green chromian + yellow-brown + pink manganvesuvianite are the four primary color varieties, all driven by trace-cation dispatch (Cu / Cr / Fe / Mn read off existing FluidChemistry fields in the engine — structurally analogous to v103 Y→fluorite + v62-era Cr→ruby pattern). References: Werner AG (1795) original type description; Allen FM & Burnham CW (1992) Am. Min. 77:268; Groat LA, Hawthorne FC, Ercit TS (1992) Can. Min. 30:19 vesuvianite crystal chemistry; Bernardini GP (1981) MR 12(5):277 Jeffrey canonical; Anthony et al. Handbook v.II; Deer Howie Zussman Rock-Forming Minerals v.1A.

Zn₂SiO₄ — trigonal R-3̄ NESOSILICATE, PHENAKITE-GROUP (isostructural with phenakite Be₂SiO₄). Hardness 5.5, density 3.89-4.20 g/cm³ (highest of the Zn supergene triad — useful field clue). Color: pure willemite colorless; Mn²⁺-substituted troostite variety apple-green to yellow-green to honey-yellow (Skorpion) to red-brown (Franklin troostite); orange-red rare. Dominated by Mn²⁺ + Fe²⁺ trace substitution in Zn site. FAMOUSLY UV-FLUORESCENT BRIGHT GREEN under SW (254 nm) UV — Mn²⁺ activator, even traces (~0.1%) produce strong response. The Franklin 'fluorescent rocks' trade rests on this single fact. Bimodal formation: PRIMARY/metamorphic at 500-600°C in the Franklin-Sterling NJ Zn-Mn skarn (Frondel 1972 troostite); OR SUPERGENE 'nonsulfide' at 50-200°C in Skorpion-Vazante-Beltana-style deposits (Hitzman et al. 2003; Brugger et al. 2003 Skorpion thermometry). The two modes are kinetically + thermodynamically distinct — supergene mode replaces sphalerite directly when SiO₂ activity is sustained high; primary mode crystallizes in Zn-Mn protolith metamorphism. Type locality Stolberg, Belgium. Substrate priority: sphalerite (supergene replacement) > smithsonite > vug wall. Refs: research dossier 2026-05; Hitzman et al. 2003 (Skorpion type section); Boni & Mondillo 2015 (nonsulfide Zn synthesis); Brugger et al. 2003; Frondel 1972 (Franklin troostite); Dana 7th v.II p.499; Handbook of Mineralogy v.III.

BaCO3 — the barium carbonate, sister to barite (BaSO4). Almost always cyclically twinned into pseudohexagonal pyramidal forms — a single un-twinned witherite crystal is unusual. Forms in low-T hydrothermal veins where Ba²⁺ encounters carbonate-rich fluids and sulfate is suppressed; loses to barite when SO4 is dominant, which is most environments. Type locality Alston Moor (Cumbria, England, 1784); William Withering (also discoverer of digitalis) named the species. Settlingstones Mine (Northumberland, England) is the world's reference for botryoidal white masses. Cave-in-Rock (Illinois) is the classic American MVT-fluorite-witherite-barite locality. Strongly UV-fluorescent (bluish-white) and persistently phosphorescent.

(Fe,Mn)WO4 — the Fe-Mn tungstate, intermediate member of the ferberite (FeWO4) ↔ hübnerite (MnWO4) solid-solution series. Specific gravity 7.0–7.5 — three times denser than quartz — is the field diagnostic. Forms in W-Sn vein systems associated with granitic intrusions, at 300–400°C in mildly acidic, reducing fluids carrying hundreds of ppm dissolved W. Loses to scheelite (CaWO4) when Ca is available, which means wolframite indicates Ca-poor conditions. Refractory: stable to very high T and chemically resistant. Does not fluoresce (diagnostic distinction from scheelite which glows blue-white under SW). Panasqueira (Portugal) is the world reference for bladed crystals on quartz; Yaogangxian (Hunan, China) supplies the modern collector market. Etymology: 'wolf's froth' — medieval miners noted that the ore consumed tin yields like a predator.

CaSiO₃ — triclinic single-chain Ca-silicate (inosilicate). The simplest Ca-Si stoichiometry of the calc-silicate suite. H 4.5-5, density 2.86-3.09, vitreous to silky luster, perfect {100} + {001} cleavage. Forms in three settings: (1) SKARN contact-metamorphism of impure limestone (the dominant occurrence — Crestmore CA, Willsboro NY, Helan Mountains China, Pakistan, Mexico Sierra de Cruces; INDUSTRIALLY mined globally as a ceramic filler + asbestos replacement at ~700,000 tonnes/year world production), (2) Rodingite metasomatism (Jeffrey Mine — acicular sprays + radiating aggregates per Bernardini 1981 MR 12(5):277; usually as the late-stage Ca-Si endmember after grossular + diopside), (3) Carbonatite alteration (rare). Pseudohexagonal twinning common. Discriminator from analogous Ca-silicates: pectolite has Na + OH (wollastonite has neither); diopside has Mg + chain doubling; grossular is the orthosilicate garnet (different structural class). Refs: Anthony Handbook v.IIB; Deer Howie Zussman 2A; Trommsdorff V & Connolly JAD (1996) The ultramafic contact aureole about the Bregaglia (Bergell) tonalite. Schweiz. Mineral. Petrogr. Mitt. 76:135 (wollastonite-isograd phase relations).

PbMoO₄, the sunset caught in stone. Thin tabular plates in honey-yellow to blood-orange. Needs oxidized Pb AND molybdate in the same zone, but the Mo is commonly a trace passenger in galena/wallrock — Red Cloud and Mežica have no discrete molybdenite. A narrow paragenetic window that makes specimens collector-prized.

(Zn,Fe)S, the hexagonal dimorph of sphalerite — same composition, different stacking. The true equilibrium inversion sits near 1020°C, so every wurtzite in a vein or vug is METASTABLE: what stabilizes it at low temperature is chemistry, not heat — sulfur-deficient, acidic fluids favor nucleating the hexagonal stacking (the simulator dispatches it above 95°C as its gameplay gate). The distinctive hemimorphic habit (one end pointed, one end flat) comes from the non-centrosymmetric P6₃mc space group. Over geologic time wurtzite converts down to sphalerite; sphalerite essentially never goes back, so surviving wurtzite is diagnostic of young or chemically-guarded growth. Type locality San José Mine (Oruro, Bolivia, tin-silver veins); Llallagua produces the best-formed crystals, Mont Saint-Hilaire alkalic pegmatites give the rare hexagonal prisms.

Cu(UO₂)₂(AsO₄)₂·(10-16)H₂O — tetragonal uranyl arsenate, the As-branch of the autunite-group anion-competition trio. Visually almost indistinguishable from torbernite — same emerald-green color, same square tabular habit, same micaceous cleavage — distinguishable only by chemistry. The arsenic is the giveaway: zeunerite localities are almost always former mining districts with arsenic-bearing primary ores (arsenopyrite, tennantite). Forms at the supergene oxidation front when uraninite weathers alongside As-rich primary sulfides; zeunerite wins the anion race when As/(P+As) > 0.5. Mohs 2.5; dehydrates irreversibly to metazeunerite (8 H₂O) above ~75°C; non-fluorescent (Cu²⁺ quenches). Type locality: Schneeberg, Saxony (1872). Sources: Pinch & Wilson 1977; research/minerals/research-zeunerite.md.
